meta.blurb: In 1491 the Americas were not empty. Tens of millions of people lived there, from Mexica city builders to Inca relay runners. Meet them, and see how many foods on your plate, like maize, potatoes and chocolate, began with them.

beats.scene: A bird's-eye view of mountains, forests and a great city
beats.summary: Opening: in 1491 the Americas were not empty but home to tens of millions of people.

beats.scene: A map of two great continents joined by a narrow neck of land
beats.summary: Two continents, North and South America, run from the frozen Arctic to the far south.

beats.scene: Farmers, fishers, hunters and city dwellers in four small scenes
beats.summary: Peoples lived in many different ways: some farmed, some fished, some hunted, some built cities.

beats.scene: Speech bubbles in many shapes rise from a crowd of different people
beats.summary: Hundreds of languages, from many unrelated families, were spoken across the Americas.

beats.scene: A sailor points at a coast while a mapmaker writes the word Indies
beats.summary: Columbus believed he had reached the Indies, which is why the word Indian stuck.

beats.scene: A scholar looks at a table of numbers with question marks
beats.summary: Nobody knows how many people lived in the Americas in 1491; estimates differ widely.

beats.scene: Diggers brush soil from old pots and tools in a trench
beats.summary: Archaeologists dig up pots, tools, bones and buildings to learn how people lived long ago.

beats.scene: An elder tells a story to children around a fire
beats.summary: Oral histories, Indigenous books and Spanish writings are other sources, each with its own limits.

beats.scene: A wide green wilderness with a far-off village that nobody notices
beats.summary: Europeans later pictured an untouched wilderness, but people had shaped the land for thousands of years.

beats.scene: Footprints in snow lead from the page toward a distant mountain
beats.summary: Preview: the story begins with the first people to arrive, long before any city was built.

beats.scene: Walls of ice and a grassy plain beside a gray sea
beats.summary: During the last ice age so much water was frozen that the sea fell and a land opened between Asia and Alaska.

beats.scene: Herds of mammoth and horses graze on a wide flat grassland under pale sun
beats.summary: Beringia, the land between Siberia and Alaska, was a wide cold grassland, not a thin bridge.

beats.scene: A small camp of hide tents sits in a windy valley below a glacier
beats.summary: Genetic evidence suggests the ancestors of Native Americans may have lived in Beringia for thousands of years.

beats.scene: A narrow gap between two cliffs of blue ice
beats.summary: Two huge ice sheets covered Canada, so an inland route south may have been closed for a long time.

beats.scene: A skin boat glides through a forest of tall golden kelp
beats.summary: The Pacific coast may have been a highway of kelp forests full of fish, seals and shellfish.

beats.scene: Two people paddle a boat of hide toward a green island
beats.summary: Boats were already in use, and people reached California's Channel Islands about thirteen thousand years ago.

beats.scene: Human footprints press into the soft mud beside an ancient lake
beats.summary: In New Mexico, footprints at White Sands may be about twenty-three thousand years old, though some scientists doubt it.

beats.scene: A camp of hide tents and wooden poles beside a stream
beats.summary: At Monte Verde in Chile, a camp about fourteen and a half thousand years old was preserved in wet peat.

beats.scene: A grooved stone spear point lies on a table beside a ruler
beats.summary: Clovis spear points, about thirteen thousand years old, were once thought to mark the first Americans.

beats.scene: A scientist holds a tiny bone beside a computer screen showing DNA patterns
beats.summary: Ancient DNA from a Montana child links the first Americans to a wide family of later peoples.

beats.scene: A giant sloth, a mastodon and a huge beaver stand in a forest
beats.summary: The Ice Age Americas held giant animals such as mammoths, mastodons, giant sloths and giant beavers.

beats.scene: A hunter uses a hooked stick to throw a long spear at a mammoth
beats.summary: Hunters used stone-tipped spears and the atlatl, a stick that threw a spear faster and farther.

beats.scene: Bones of a mammoth lie scattered in dry earth beneath a pale sky
beats.summary: Most of the big animals disappeared between about thirteen and ten thousand years ago, and the reason is debated.

beats.scene: Melting glaciers feed a river as green plants spread across a valley
beats.summary: About twelve thousand years ago the ice age ended and the warmer world changed the land.

beats.scene: A stone spear point sticks in the rib of a large old bison
beats.summary: At Folsom in New Mexico, a spear point found among the bones of an extinct bison showed how old human life in America was.

beats.scene: Hunters hide behind rocks as bison run toward a high cliff
beats.summary: Plains hunters drove bison over cliffs, known as buffalo jumps, which were used for thousands of years.

beats.scene: Women pound acorns in a stone bowl beside a river in California
beats.summary: Californian peoples gathered acorns, leached them and ground them into meal, and fed large communities without farming.

beats.scene: A mound of white shells taller than a house stands beside a bay
beats.summary: Along the coasts, people piled up shell mounds, some of them as tall as houses and thousands of years old.

beats.scene: A woman weaves a tight basket while another gathers pine nuts in a desert
beats.summary: Desert peoples lived on seeds, pine nuts and small animals, and wove baskets fine enough to carry water.

beats.scene: Small groups of people stand on a mountain, coast, plain and riverbank
beats.summary: By about ten thousand years ago people lived in nearly every part of the Americas, and many languages grew.

beats.scene: A thin wild grass with few hard seeds beside a fat corn ear
beats.summary: Teosinte, a wild grass of southern Mexico, has only a few hard seeds and looks nothing like corn.

beats.scene: Gatherers collect seeds from tall grass in a river valley
beats.summary: Farmers in the Balsas River valley of southern Mexico began changing teosinte about nine thousand years ago.

beats.scene: Hands compare a tiny old corn cob with a modern ear
beats.summary: The first cobs were smaller than a thumb; farmers saved the best seed and made them larger over thousands of years.

beats.scene: Ears of corn in blue, red, yellow, white and speckled colours fill a basket
beats.summary: Farmers developed dozens of kinds of corn in many colours, each suited to its own soil and climate.

beats.scene: A woman soaks corn kernels in a pot of water and white ash
beats.summary: Soaking corn in water with lime or ash, called nixtamalization, makes it tastier and more nourishing.

beats.scene: A farmer drops seeds of beans into a hole beside a young corn plant
beats.summary: Beans were farmed in Mexico and the Andes, and with corn they gave people a balanced diet.

beats.scene: Corn stalks hold up climbing bean vines while big squash leaves cover the ground
beats.summary: The Three Sisters: corn gave beans a pole, beans fed the soil, and squash leaves shaded out weeds.

beats.scene: A line of farmers carry seed bags across mountains, desert and forest
beats.summary: Maize travelled north and south, reaching the Andes, the Southwest, and later the eastern woodlands.

beats.scene: A Hopi farmer plants corn deep in dry red sand beneath a mesa
beats.summary: Farmers adapted corn to short summers, high mountains and deserts, as Hopi farmers did by planting it deep.

beats.scene: A child holds an ear of corn beside a stalk under a golden sun
beats.summary: Maize is now one of the most widely grown crops in the world, and sacred in many Indigenous traditions.

beats.scene: A farmer digs small wild potatoes from stony ground near a blue lake
beats.summary: Potatoes were first farmed in the Andes near Lake Titicaca about eight thousand years ago.

beats.scene: A table of potatoes in purple, red, yellow and spotted shapes
beats.summary: Andean farmers grew thousands of kinds of potato in many colours and shapes, at many heights.

beats.scene: Women trample potatoes on frosty ground under a clear night sky
beats.summary: Freeze-dried potatoes called chuno could be stored for years.

beats.scene: A field of quinoa with red and gold heads beneath snowy mountains
beats.summary: Quinoa, a protein-rich seed, grew high in the Andes where wheat could not.

beats.scene: A cook cuts a ripe red tomato beside a stone grinding bowl
beats.summary: Tomatoes were grown in Mexico, and their name comes from the Nahuatl word tomatl.

beats.scene: Strings of red and green chillies hang drying beside a clay pot
beats.summary: Chillies were grown for thousands of years in the Americas and carried to the rest of the world after 1492.

beats.scene: A golden cacao pod hangs from a tree trunk in a rainforest
beats.summary: Cacao came from the upper Amazon; people in Ecuador were using it about 5,300 years ago.

beats.scene: A Maya woman pours frothy chocolate from one jar to another
beats.summary: In Mesoamerica chocolate was a bitter, frothy drink flavoured with chillies and flowers, with no sugar.

beats.scene: A pile of cassava roots and peanuts beside a river village
beats.summary: Cassava, peanuts and other crops came from South America's lowlands and fed millions of people.

beats.scene: A table of avocados, pineapples, vanilla pods, sunflowers and cotton bolls
beats.summary: Avocado, pineapple, vanilla, sunflowers and cotton also came from the Americas, and Europe had none of them.

beats.scene: A herder leads a line of llamas carrying bundles along a mountain path
beats.summary: Llamas were bred in the Andes about six thousand years ago and carried loads in long caravans.

beats.scene: Alpacas with thick wool graze on a green meadow beside a stream
beats.summary: Alpacas gave fine wool, and wild vicunas gave the finest of all, which was kept for royalty.

beats.scene: A skeleton of a small ancient horse stands in a museum case
beats.summary: Horses lived in the Americas long ago but died out, and the Spanish brought them back after 1492.

beats.scene: A woman bends under a heavy bundle held by a strap across her forehead
beats.summary: Without cattle or horses, people carried heavy loads themselves, often with a strap across the forehead.

beats.scene: A small clay animal with wheels stands on a cloth beside a pot
beats.summary: Mesoamerican children had toys with wheels, but wheels were not used for carts because there were no animals to pull them.

beats.scene: A hairy white dog with a thick coat stands beside a loom
beats.summary: Dogs came with the first Americans, and the Coast Salish kept a special woolly dog for its fleece.

beats.scene: A flock of turkeys scratch in a courtyard beside a stone house
beats.summary: Turkeys were raised in Mexico and in the Southwest for meat, and their feathers made blankets.

beats.scene: Small guinea pigs run across the floor of a stone kitchen
beats.summary: Guinea pigs, called cuy, were raised in Andean homes for food and for ceremonies.

beats.scene: Reed boats float on a blue lake while a balsa raft sails the sea
beats.summary: Peoples built dugout canoes, birchbark canoes, reed boats and balsa rafts that sailed the coast.

beats.scene: Traders with bundles of shells, blue stones and feathers meet on a trail
beats.summary: Trade networks carried shells, obsidian, turquoise and feathers over great distances.

beats.scene: Low stone platforms and a sunken round plaza stand in a dry Peruvian valley
beats.summary: Caral, in the Supe valley of Peru, about five thousand years old, is one of the oldest cities in the Americas.

beats.scene: Six stepped platform mounds rise around a sunken circle of stone
beats.summary: Caral had large stepped platforms and a sunken round plaza, and no known pottery or writing.

beats.scene: Farmers carry cotton and squash to fishers who hold nets of fish
beats.summary: Farmers grew cotton and food; fishers on the coast caught anchovies and sardines and traded fish for cotton.

beats.scene: A musician plays a flute made of bone on a stone platform
beats.summary: Thirty-two flutes made of bird bones were found at Caral, showing the importance of music.

beats.scene: A stone temple with a dark doorway and a carved fanged god
beats.summary: Chavin de Huantar, a mountain temple about three thousand years old, drew pilgrims from all over the Andes.

beats.scene: A mummy bundle wrapped in embroidered cloth lies in a desert grave
beats.summary: Paracas people of the dry south coast wrapped their dead in magnificent embroidered textiles about two thousand years ago.

beats.scene: A huge hummingbird figure drawn on a pale desert plain seen from above
beats.summary: The Nazca lines are giant drawings of animals and shapes on the Peruvian desert, made by removing dark stones.

beats.scene: A spiral stone opening leads down into a tunnel beside a dry field
beats.summary: The Nazca also built underground channels, called puquios, that brought water to their fields, some of which still work.

beats.scene: A huge mud-brick pyramid stands beside a river with painted pots in front
beats.summary: The Moche built great mud-brick pyramids and canals on the north coast of Peru and made lifelike portrait pots.

beats.scene: A golden ear ornament and a necklace glitter in a tomb among clay pots
beats.summary: In 1987 a Moche tomb at Sipan was found with its rich burial of a ruler untouched by thieves.

beats.scene: A river winds through hot wet lowlands where a village stands in the trees
beats.summary: The Olmec lived on the hot, wet Gulf coast of Mexico from about 3,200 to 2,400 years ago.

beats.scene: A giant stone head in a round helmet stands in a jungle clearing
beats.summary: Seventeen colossal Olmec heads are known, each carved from a single block of basalt.

beats.scene: Workers drag a huge stone on a raft of logs across a wide river
beats.summary: The basalt came from mountains many miles away, and how it was moved without wheels or draft animals is not fully known.

beats.scene: A ruler in a headdress sits on a throne of stone before kneeling people
beats.summary: Most scholars think the heads show Olmec rulers, who had power over many workers.

beats.scene: Workers cut milky sap from a rubber tree beside a heap of dark balls
beats.summary: The Olmec and their neighbours made rubber from tree sap, and Europeans had never seen it before.

beats.scene: Players with padded belts strike a heavy rubber ball in a stone court
beats.summary: The Mesoamerican ballgame was played in stone courts with a heavy rubber ball, often with great ritual meaning.

beats.scene: A small jade figure with a baby face lies on cloth
beats.summary: Olmec artists carved fine jade figures with babyish faces, and their art influenced later peoples.

beats.scene: A stone slab covered in rows of small signs lies on a lab table
beats.summary: The Cascajal Block, found in 1999, has signs that some scholars think are the oldest writing in the Americas.

beats.scene: A flat-topped mountain with stone temples and a plaza above a green valley
beats.summary: The Zapotec built Monte Alban on a levelled mountaintop in Oaxaca, about 500 BC, and it stayed a capital for over a thousand years.

beats.scene: People of different villages exchange pottery, jade and seeds at a crossroads
beats.summary: Mesoamerica shared maize, ballgames, calendars and pyramids across many peoples who spoke different languages.

beats.scene: A map of green forest with many small cities marked by pyramids
beats.summary: The Maya lived in southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and nearby lands, in many separate city-states.

beats.scene: A giant stepped pyramid rises above a thick green jungle at dawn
beats.summary: El Mirador in Guatemala grew into a huge city more than two thousand years ago, with a pyramid among the largest ever built.

beats.scene: Tall temples with steep stairs poke out above the tree tops at sunrise
beats.summary: Tikal in Guatemala was a great classic Maya city with temples rising above the forest, about 250 to 900.

beats.scene: Two kings in feather headdresses stand with spears on opposite hills
beats.summary: Maya kings led their cities in ritual and war, and strong cities such as Tikal and Calakmul had rivalries and allies.

beats.scene: A stone coffin lid carved with a king falling into a jaws-shaped world
beats.summary: In 1952 the tomb of King Pakal of Palenque was found inside a pyramid, with a jade mask and a carved stone lid.

beats.scene: A queen in a long robe and a headdress stands on a stone platform
beats.summary: Several Maya women ruled cities as queens, among them Lady Yohl Iknal of Palenque and Lady Six Sky of Naranjo.

beats.scene: Rainwater flows into a stone-lined reservoir beside a limestone cave pool
beats.summary: The Maya stored rainwater in reservoirs and used sacred sinkholes called cenotes, because the lowlands have few rivers.

beats.scene: A farmer clears a small field beside a thatched house
beats.summary: Most Maya were farmers who grew maize, beans and squash and lived in houses of poles and thatch around the temple centres.

beats.scene: Painted walls show a king, musicians and warriors in a small stone room
beats.summary: Painted murals at Bonampak, about 790, show Maya court life, music and war in bright colours.

beats.scene: A potter paints a bright design of a god on a tall clay cylinder
beats.summary: Maya pottery was painted in many colours with scenes of gods and rulers, and sometimes signed by the artists.

beats.scene: Carved stone blocks covered in small square symbols
beats.summary: Maya writing used hundreds of picture signs, some for words and some for sounds, arranged in square blocks.

beats.scene: A scholar compares sketches of signs with a map of a ruined city
beats.summary: Scholars slowly learned to read Maya writing in the twentieth century, led by Knorozov and Proskouriakoff.

beats.scene: A friar throws painted bark books into a fire in a village square
beats.summary: Maya painted books were burned in 1562 by a Spanish friar, and only four survive.

beats.scene: A wide stone stairway covered with carved signs climbs a temple
beats.summary: The stairway at Copan carries about 2,200 signs, the longest Maya text.

beats.scene: A shell sign for zero stands beside a row of dots and bars
beats.summary: The Maya used dots, bars and a shell sign for zero in a counting system based on twenty.

beats.scene: Two great wheels with sun and day signs turn together on a stone wall
beats.summary: The Maya had two calendars, one of 260 days and one of 365, which together made a cycle of 52 years.

beats.scene: A priest points at a bright planet over a temple
beats.summary: The Maya tracked Venus very accurately and predicted eclipses, writing their tables in books.

beats.scene: A calendar stone rolls over like an odometer at the end of a cycle
beats.summary: The Long Count cycle that ended in December 2012 did not predict the end of the world; it simply began a new cycle.

beats.scene: A young noble scribe paints a book beside a pot of ink
beats.summary: Scribes were respected, and many came from noble families; some were princes.

beats.scene: Two brothers play a ballgame against skeleton lords in a dark underworld
beats.summary: The Popol Vuh, written in the 1500s by Maya authors, tells how the Hero Twins beat the Lords of Death at ball.

beats.scene: A wide avenue lined with temples leads toward a huge pyramid at sunrise
beats.summary: Teotihuacan, near Mexico City, was a planned city that held 100,000 people or more around the year 500.

beats.scene: A very long straight road runs between low temples toward two pyramids
beats.summary: The Avenue of the Dead ran more than two kilometres through the city between temples and palaces.

beats.scene: A giant stepped pyramid rises beside a smaller pyramid
beats.summary: The Pyramid of the Sun, about sixty-five metres high, is one of the largest buildings of the ancient Americas.

beats.scene: A stone pyramid carved with serpent heads and a narrow tunnel beneath it
beats.summary: Under the Pyramid of the Feathered Serpent, archaeologists found a long tunnel with rich offerings in 2003.

beats.scene: Rows of walled stone houses with painted red walls and courtyards
beats.summary: Most people lived in walled apartment compounds with painted walls, sharing courtyards with their relatives and neighbours.

beats.scene: A noble in a feathered headdress arrives at a city gate with soldiers
beats.summary: In 378, a foreign lord linked to Teotihuacan arrived at Tikal, and a new line of kings followed.

beats.scene: A burning temple and a crowd leaving a great city at night
beats.summary: Around 550 the centre of Teotihuacan was burned, and the city declined, though people stayed for centuries.

beats.scene: Dry grass and cracked earth beneath a hot sun near a ruined temple
beats.summary: Around 800 to 900, many Maya cities stopped building and emptied; drought, war and other troubles all played a part.

beats.scene: A pyramid with four stairways and a long snaking shadow
beats.summary: Chichen Itza in the north rose around 900 and became a great trading city with a famous pyramid and ball court.

beats.scene: Women in white embroidered dresses weave on a loom outside a village house
beats.summary: The Maya never vanished; millions of Maya people live today in Mexico, Guatemala and Belize and speak Mayan languages.

beats.scene: A long line of snowy peaks above a terraced green valley
beats.summary: Before the Inca, the Andes saw earlier states such as Tiwanaku near Lake Titicaca and Wari in Peru.

beats.scene: A vast adobe city of walls and courtyards decorated with fish and waves
beats.summary: Chan Chan, the capital of the Chimu kingdom, was the largest mud-brick city in the Americas, until the Inca conquered it about 1470.

beats.scene: A small walled town and fields in a high valley
beats.summary: Cusco was a small town in a high valley that grew into the capital of the Inca, who told stories of their origins.

beats.scene: A wall of defenders and warriors fight a dusty battle outside a city
beats.summary: About 1438, Pachacuti defended Cusco against the Chanka and then began to build the empire.

beats.scene: A map of the Andes with four coloured quarters meeting at Cusco
beats.summary: Pachacuti, his son Topa Inca and his grandson Huayna Capac built Tawantinsuyu, which ran about four thousand kilometres.

beats.scene: A ruler greets a local lord with a gift of cloth while soldiers wait
beats.summary: The Inca ruled by conquest, gifts and moving families, and made Quechua the shared language.

beats.scene: A ruler on a litter wears a bright tunic and a red fringe
beats.summary: The Sapa Inca was called Son of the Sun, and dead rulers were mummified and kept as honoured members of the court.

beats.scene: A great temple with gold-covered walls faces the rising sun
beats.summary: The Inca honoured the Sun god Inti, the creator Viracocha, and Pachamama, and their temple in Cusco was lavish.

beats.scene: Dancers in bright cloth and feathers fill a plaza at dawn
beats.summary: At the winter solstice the Inca held the festival of Inti Raymi, which is celebrated in Cusco today.

beats.scene: A weaver sits at a loom with bright wool while a goldsmith works nearby
beats.summary: The Inca valued fine cloth as much as gold, using it for gifts, rewards and ceremonies.

beats.scene: A paved stone road with steps climbs a steep mountain beneath a cloudy sky
beats.summary: The Inca built more than thirty thousand kilometres of roads over mountains, deserts and jungle.

beats.scene: A rope bridge made of woven grass hangs over a deep river gorge
beats.summary: Inca engineers wove huge rope bridges from grass, and a bridge at Q'eswachaka is still rebuilt each year.

beats.scene: A runner blows a shell horn and hands a cord to another
beats.summary: Relay runners called chasqui carried messages along the roads, passing them on at stations every few kilometres.

beats.scene: A thatched stone house beside a mountain road with food stores
beats.summary: Roadside stations called tambos gave travellers food and a place to sleep, and supplied armies and officials.

beats.scene: An official ties knots in a coloured cord at a stone table
beats.summary: The Inca kept records with the quipu, knotted cords that recorded numbers and possibly more.

beats.scene: A family works a field while an official watches with a quipu in hand
beats.summary: The mita was a labour tax in which families worked for the state, which in return fed and rewarded the workers.

beats.scene: Long rows of small stone storehouses stand on a windy hillside
beats.summary: Thousands of storehouses held food, cloth and tools, helping the empire survive bad harvests.

beats.scene: Green stone terraces climb the sides of a steep valley
beats.summary: Stone terraces turned steep mountainsides into farmland, and the circular terraces of Moray may have been used for growing experiments.

beats.scene: A wall of huge stones fitted together without a gap beneath a cloudy sky
beats.summary: Inca stonemasons fitted giant blocks together without mortar, and their walls have survived many earthquakes.

beats.scene: Stone houses and terraces cling to a ridge above clouds and a river
beats.summary: Machu Picchu, built about 1450, was a royal estate high above a river, and it was made known to the world in 1911.

beats.scene: A band of travellers with bundles and children trudges toward a blue lake
beats.summary: The Mexica, called Aztecs by later writers, came to the Valley of Mexico as poor latecomers around the thirteenth century.

beats.scene: An eagle perches on a cactus on a small island in a lake
beats.summary: The Mexica said their god told them to settle where they saw an eagle on a cactus, and they founded Tenochtitlan about 1325.

beats.scene: Workers build a long stone road across the water toward an island city
beats.summary: The Mexica built causeways, dikes and canals, and brought drinking water by aqueduct from the shore.

beats.scene: Spanish soldiers stare in wonder at a white city shining on a lake
beats.summary: By 1519 Tenochtitlan held perhaps two hundred thousand people, and the Spanish who saw it were amazed.

beats.scene: Farmers pole narrow boats beside small garden plots full of vegetables
beats.summary: Chinampas, raised garden plots built in the shallow lake, gave several harvests a year and fed the city.

beats.scene: A crowded square with stalls of cloth, feathers, pottery and food
beats.summary: The Tlatelolco market was huge, with tens of thousands of visitors and cacao beans used as small change.

beats.scene: Three rulers on mats sign a pact with maps of cities behind them
beats.summary: In 1428 Tenochtitlan joined Texcoco and Tlacopan in the Triple Alliance, and the empire grew by conquest and tribute.

beats.scene: Boys sit in rows learning from a teacher beside a temple
beats.summary: Many Aztec boys went to school, and nobles' sons went to a separate school that trained leaders and priests.

beats.scene: A huge round stone carved with a sun face and calendar signs
beats.summary: The Stone of the Sun, found in 1790 under Mexico City, shows the Aztec view of time and the world.

beats.scene: A twin-peaked white temple stands above a plaza full of smoke
beats.summary: The Templo Mayor was the centre of Aztec religion, and human sacrifice was real, though Spanish writers often exaggerated its scale.

beats.scene: A ring of grassy mounds around a flat clearing in a marshy forest
beats.summary: At Watson Brake in Louisiana, hunters built a ring of earth mounds about five thousand years ago.

beats.scene: Curved ridges of earth rise in half circles around an open plaza
beats.summary: Poverty Point in Louisiana, about 3,400 years old, has six half-circle ridges built by hunter-gatherers who traded far and wide.

beats.scene: A circular earthwork joined to a square one in a green Ohio field
beats.summary: The Hopewell peoples of the Ohio valley built burial mounds and great geometric earthworks about two thousand years ago.

beats.scene: A viewer stands inside an octagon of earth banks watching the moon rise
beats.summary: The Newark Earthworks in Ohio line up with the moon's long cycle of eighteen and a half years, and became a World Heritage Site in 2023.

beats.scene: Traders lay copper, shells, mica and bear teeth on a cloth
beats.summary: Hopewell traders gathered copper, mica, shells, obsidian and other precious things from across the continent.

beats.scene: Tall earth mounds rise above houses and fields beside a wide river
beats.summary: Cahokia, near the Mississippi in Illinois, grew rapidly after about 1050 and became the largest city north of Mexico.

beats.scene: A huge flat-topped earth mound with stairs and a temple on its summit
beats.summary: Monks Mound, about thirty metres high, is the largest earthen mound in the Americas and was built from baskets of soil.

beats.scene: A ring of tall wooden posts stands as the sun rises
beats.summary: Cahokia's wooden circles, called Woodhenge, marked the sun's seasons, and people played the chunkey game on the plaza.

beats.scene: A grave with thousands of shell beads laid out like a bird
beats.summary: In Mound 72, a ruler was buried on thousands of shell beads, with many other people, which suggests human sacrifice.

beats.scene: Empty houses and a wooden wall stand silent on a grey flooded plain
beats.summary: By about 1350 Cahokia was empty, perhaps because of floods, droughts, war and a lack of wood, long before Columbus.

beats.scene: Red cliffs rise above a dry canyon with a small green field
beats.summary: The Ancestral Pueblo peoples farmed the dry Southwest, growing corn, beans and squash with little rain.

beats.scene: A great curved building of stone with many rooms stands in a dry canyon
beats.summary: Pueblo Bonito at Chaco Canyon in New Mexico was a vast stone building with hundreds of rooms, built in stages from about 850 to 1150.

beats.scene: A narrow beam of sunlight crosses a spiral carved on a rock wall
beats.summary: At Chaco, buildings and rock carvings were lined up with the sun and moon, such as the Sun Dagger on Fajada Butte.

beats.scene: A long straight road runs across a desert toward distant cliffs
beats.summary: The Chaco roads were wide and straight, running for many miles from the canyon without wheels or horses.

beats.scene: A bright macaw sits beside a jar for chocolate in a stone room
beats.summary: Chaco's buildings held macaw feathers, chocolate and turquoise from far away, and its roofs used thousands of timbers carried from the mountains.

beats.scene: A dry gully and cracked soil beside empty stone houses in a canyon
beats.summary: Around 1150 a long drought led people to leave Chaco, though it stayed a sacred place.

beats.scene: A village of stone rooms and round towers fills a shelf under a cliff
beats.summary: At Mesa Verde in Colorado, people built cliff dwellings from about 1190, such as Cliff Palace with about 150 rooms.

beats.scene: A family walks away from a cliff village carrying bundles and corn
beats.summary: After a great drought around 1276 to 1299, the cliff villages were left, and the people moved south.

beats.scene: A wide canal carries water through a dry desert field of corn
beats.summary: The Hohokam of southern Arizona dug hundreds of miles of canals to water their desert fields.

beats.scene: A pueblo of earth-coloured houses rises in tiers against a mountain
beats.summary: Taos Pueblo in New Mexico has been lived in for about a thousand years and is a World Heritage Site.

beats.scene: A village of bark houses and cornfields stands inside a wooden fence among forests
beats.summary: In the Eastern Woodlands, peoples such as the Haudenosaunee, Cherokee and Wampanoag farmed and hunted in villages and towns.

beats.scene: A long bark house with a rounded roof and smoke rising from several holes
beats.summary: The Haudenosaunee, People of the Longhouse, lived in long bark houses that sheltered many related families.

beats.scene: Women stand in a cornfield while an elder speaks to some men
beats.summary: Among the Haudenosaunee, descent was through the mother, women owned the fields and clan mothers chose the chiefs.

beats.scene: Two men at a council fire, one holding a belt of beads
beats.summary: Oral tradition tells how the Peacemaker and Hiawatha united five warring nations; the date is uncertain.

beats.scene: Chiefs sit in a circle beneath a tall white pine tree
beats.summary: The Great Law of Peace set up a council of fifty chiefs and a Tree of Peace under which weapons were buried.

beats.scene: A long belt of purple and white shell beads lies across a woman's hands
beats.summary: Wampum belts made of shell beads recorded treaties and laws and helped speakers remember them.

beats.scene: Speakers rise one at a time while others listen in a longhouse
beats.summary: The Haudenosaunee councils sought agreement by discussion, and each gathering began with a Thanksgiving Address to the natural world.

beats.scene: A line of low fire creeps through an open woodland as people watch
beats.summary: Many peoples burned the undergrowth to keep woods open, helping nut trees, berries and deer.

beats.scene: People in canoes bend over wild rice plants at the edge of a lake
beats.summary: Peoples of the northern lakes harvested wild rice from canoes, and others burned prairies to keep grassland for bison.

beats.scene: Armoured horsemen ride through a large town of houses around a plaza
beats.summary: In 1539 to 1543, the Spanish explorer de Soto saw large Southeastern towns, many of which had vanished by the time the next Europeans came.

beats.scene: Salmon leap up a rushing river beneath tall cedar trees
beats.summary: On the Northwest Coast, from Alaska to Oregon, runs of salmon and forests of cedar fed rich societies without farming.

beats.scene: Men split a huge cedar plank from a standing tree beside a long canoe
beats.summary: Cedar gave plank houses, great canoes, clothing and boxes, and was carved with great skill.

beats.scene: Tall carved poles with faces of eagles, bears and ravens beside a plank house
beats.summary: Totem poles carved with family crests told stories and honoured people.

beats.scene: Hosts give blankets and carved boxes to guests in a crowded plank house
beats.summary: At a potlatch, hosts gave gifts to guests, who witnessed important events; governments later banned it, but it survived.

beats.scene: People in sealskin clothes stand beside a turf house by a snowy bay
beats.summary: Ancestors of the Inuit spread across the Arctic from Alaska to Greenland about a thousand years ago.

beats.scene: A hunter paddles a slim sealskin kayak between icebergs
beats.summary: The Inuit made kayaks of sealskin on a wooden or whalebone frame and also warm clothing from skins and fur.

beats.scene: A hunter waits beside a hole in the sea ice with a harpoon
beats.summary: Inuit hunters understood ice, wind and stars so well that they could find their way and hunt in the long winter.

beats.scene: Houses, gardens and fruit trees line a wide river in a tropical forest
beats.summary: The Amazon was not an empty jungle: farming villages with plazas and roads lived along its rivers, especially in the Upper Xingu region.

beats.scene: A hand holds dark rich soil beside a bowl of broken pottery and charcoal
beats.summary: Terra preta, a dark fertile soil made by Amazon peoples from charcoal, bones and pottery, stays rich for centuries.

beats.scene: Squares and circles of long ditches lie in a cleared forest seen from above
beats.summary: Earthworks in the western Amazon and many useful trees show that people shaped the rainforest for thousands of years.

beats.scene: A wooden longship rests on a northern shore beside turf-walled houses
beats.summary: Norse sailors from Greenland built a small camp at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland about the year 1000.

beats.scene: A Norse boat leaves a beach as local people watch from the trees
beats.summary: The Norse stayed only a few years and left, so the Americas and Europe remained apart.

beats.scene: A sailor holds a round globe beside a map of the Atlantic Ocean
beats.summary: In 1492, Columbus persuaded the Spanish king and queen to pay for a voyage west to Asia, because he thought the earth was smaller than it is.

beats.scene: Three small wooden ships sail on a rolling sea under a red evening sky
beats.summary: Columbus left Spain in August 1492 with three ships, the Nina, the Pinta and the Santa Maria.

beats.scene: Three ships anchor off a green island as people gather on the beach
beats.summary: On October 12, 1492, Columbus landed in the Bahamas, on an island whose people, the Taino, called it Guanahani.

beats.scene: Villagers sit in hammocks outside round houses beside canoes on a beach
beats.summary: The Taino lived in villages led by chiefs, farmed cassava and gave English words such as canoe, hammock and hurricane.

beats.scene: A Spanish sailor and a Taino man trade cloth and a parrot
beats.summary: Columbus met friendly people, who gave gifts, but he looked for gold and took some people away by force.

beats.scene: A fleet of many ships with horses and cattle on deck leaves a harbour
beats.summary: In 1493 Columbus returned with seventeen ships, horses, cattle, pigs and settlers, and a new age began.

beats.scene: A sick man lies under a blanket as a worried healer sits beside him
beats.summary: Europeans carried smallpox, measles and flu, diseases that the people of the Americas had never met and could not resist.

beats.scene: A small empty island village with overgrown fields and a few people walking away
beats.summary: On Hispaniola the Taino population fell sharply within decades, from disease, forced labour and violence.

beats.scene: Spanish ships and a woman translator stand on a beach with local leaders
beats.summary: In 1519 Hernan Cortes landed on the Mexican coast with about five hundred men and joined with local peoples who were enemies of the Mexica.

beats.scene: A ruler in a feathered cloak meets a bearded soldier on a long causeway
beats.summary: In November 1519 Moctezuma welcomed Cortes to Tenochtitlan, but within days the Spanish took him prisoner.

beats.scene: A crowd fights on a bridge at night as people flee along a causeway
beats.summary: In 1520 fighting broke out, the Spanish fled on the Night of Sorrows, and smallpox then struck the city.

beats.scene: Boats and soldiers attack a burning city on a lake at dawn
beats.summary: In 1521 Cortes and tens of thousands of Indigenous allies besieged Tenochtitlan, which fell in August after about seventy-five days.

beats.scene: Armoured riders face a king carried on a litter
beats.summary: In 1532 Pizarro captured the Inca ruler Atahualpa, whose empire had been weakened by disease and a civil war.

beats.scene: A hidden mountain town with thatched roofs above a green river valley
beats.summary: Inca leaders resisted from the hidden stronghold of Vilcabamba until 1572, and Inca culture survived in the Andes.

beats.scene: Green forest spreads across abandoned fields in the afternoon light
beats.summary: In the worst-hit regions most people died within a century; some scientists think regrowing forests cooled the climate, though this is debated.

beats.scene: A scientist beside a laser scanner looks at a computer map of jungle ruins
beats.summary: New tools such as lidar, DNA studies and tree rings, working alongside oral histories, are changing what we know about the old Americas.

beats.scene: A smiling family in modern clothes shows woven cloth at a market stall
beats.summary: Indigenous peoples live on today, tens of millions strong, speaking languages such as Quechua, Guarani, Nahuatl and Mayan languages.

beats.scene: A child holds a potato and an ear of corn beside an old map
beats.summary: Closing: the Americas did not begin in 1492; the world still eats their foods and should know their story.

A1A2: Many people lived in America long before the ships came.
Two huge continents run from the cold north to the far south.
Some people farmed, some fished, some hunted, and some lived in cities.
People spoke hundreds of different languages, and many are still spoken today.
Columbus thought he had reached India, so he called the people Indians.
Nobody knows exactly how many people lived there in 1491.
Workers dig up old pots and tools from deep in the ground.
Many peoples kept their history by telling stories from parent to child.
Later visitors thought the land was wild, but people had shaped it.
Let us begin with the very first people to arrive.
In the ice age, so much water was ice that the sea fell.
Between Asia and Alaska there was a wide, cold, grassy plain.
Some of the first travellers may have lived there for many years.
Two huge walls of ice blocked the way south for a long time.
A boat could follow the coast, where the sea gave plenty of food.
By about thirteen thousand years ago, people were sailing to islands.
In New Mexico, people left footprints in mud beside a lake.
At Monte Verde in Chile, people once lived beside a small stream.
Hunters made fine stone spear points about thirteen thousand years ago.
Old bones can show us how the first Americans were related.
Giant animals once walked through the forests and over the plains.
A hunter used a special stick to throw a spear far.
Then, one by one, the big animals all disappeared.
About twelve thousand years ago, the world became warmer.
A spear point was found among old bones of a giant bison.
Some hunters drove bison over a cliff to get meat.
In California, women ground acorns into flour to make food.
People ate many sea animals and piled the shells into big hills.
In dry lands, people gathered seeds and nuts and made baskets.
By ten thousand years ago, people lived almost everywhere in the Americas.
Corn began as a thin wild grass with only a few seeds.
In southern Mexico, people began to plant this grass long ago.
The first ears of corn were very small, like a thumb.
Farmers grew corn in many colours, such as blue, red and yellow.
Women soaked corn in water with lime, and then made dough.
Beans grew beside the corn, and together they fed many people.
Corn, beans and squash were planted together in the same field.
Corn travelled north and south as people shared seeds and ideas.
Farmers changed corn so it could grow in dry lands.
Today corn is one of the most important foods in the world.
Farmers in the Andes began to grow potatoes long ago.
Andean farmers grew thousands of kinds of potato in many colours.
Andean people left potatoes outside in the frost and the sun.
Quinoa is a small seed that grows high up in the mountains.
In Mexico, people grew red tomatoes and put them in many dishes.
Chillies were very popular, and farmers grew many different kinds.
Chocolate comes from the seeds of a tree that grows in warm forests.
People in Mexico drank bitter chocolate, with no sugar in it.
In the warm, low land, people grew cassava and peanuts for food.
Many other plants came from the Americas too, such as avocados.
In the Andes, people used llamas to carry heavy loads.
Alpacas gave people soft wool to make warm clothes.
There were no horses in the Americas in 1491.
Without big animals, people carried heavy loads on their own backs.
In Mexico, children played with little clay toys that had wheels.
Dogs came to the Americas with the early people.
People kept turkeys for their meat and for their feathers.
In the Andes, families kept guinea pigs in their homes.
People built canoes and rafts to travel on rivers and seas.
Traders carried shells, stones and feathers over great distances.
Caral in Peru is about five thousand years old.
Caral had big stone platforms with steps and a round plaza.
Farmers grew cotton, and fishers on the coast caught many fish.
People at Caral played flutes made from the bones of birds.
Chavin de Huantar was a famous temple in the mountains.
In the dry south of Peru, people wrapped the dead in fine cloth.
In the desert of Peru, people drew giant pictures of animals.
The Nazca people also dug tunnels to bring water to their fields.
The Moche people built huge pyramids from mud bricks.
In 1987, workers found the rich tomb of a Moche lord.
The Olmec lived in the hot, wet lands of eastern Mexico.
The Olmec carved huge stone heads that people can still see.
The stone came from mountains far away, and nobody knows exactly how.
Most experts think each head shows a powerful Olmec ruler.
People in Mexico made rubber from the white sap of a tree.
Players hit a heavy rubber ball with their hips in a stone court.
Olmec artists carved small figures from beautiful green jade stone.
A stone slab with strange signs was found in Mexico in 1999.
The Zapotec people built a city on top of a mountain.
Many peoples in Mexico shared similar foods, games and ideas.
Maya cities stood in the hot forests of Mexico and Guatemala.
Long ago, the Maya built a huge city called El Mirador.
Tikal was a famous Maya city with tall stone temples.
Maya kings fought wars and led holy ceremonies in their cities.
At Palenque, the tomb of King Pakal was found inside a temple.
Some Maya cities were ruled by queens, not by kings.
The Maya saved rain in big tanks for the dry months.
Most Maya people were farmers who lived in simple houses.
Bonampak has beautiful paintings of kings, music and war.
Maya potters painted pots with gods, kings and beautiful patterns.
The Maya wrote with small picture signs, carved in stone.
In modern times, scholars learned how to read Maya writing.
Spanish priests burned most of the Maya books in the 1500s.
The stairway at Copan is covered with writing carved in stone.
The Maya counted with dots, bars and a sign for zero.
The Maya had two calendars that turned together like wheels.
Maya priests watched the planet Venus very carefully.
In 2012, a long Maya count ended, but the world did not.
Writers were respected, and many came from families of nobles.
The Popol Vuh tells of two brothers who beat the lords of death.
Teotihuacan was a huge planned city near today's Mexico City.
A long straight road ran through the middle of the city.
The Pyramid of the Sun is one of the largest in the world.
Under one pyramid, workers found a long tunnel full of treasures.
Most people lived in stone houses joined around open courtyards.
In 378, a lord from far away came to Tikal.
Around the year 550, the heart of Teotihuacan burned.
Between 800 and 900, many Maya cities were left empty.
In the north, a new city called Chichen Itza grew strong.
The Maya never disappeared, and millions of them live today.
Before the Inca, other great peoples lived in the Andes.
Chan Chan, the Chimu capital, was built entirely of mud bricks.
Cusco was a small town in a high mountain valley.
About 1438, an army attacked Cusco, but Pachacuti beat it.
The Inca ruled a huge land they called the Four Parts.
The Inca used war and gifts to bring new peoples in.
The ruler, called the Sapa Inca, was a son of the Sun.
The Inca prayed to the Sun, which they called Inti.
Each year the Inca held a great festival for the Sun.
The Inca prized fine cloth even more than gold.
The Inca built thousands of miles of roads through the mountains.
Builders made rope bridges from grass to cross deep canyons.
Runners called chasqui carried messages along the roads.
Along the roads, there were houses where travellers could rest.
Officials used cords with knots to keep their records.
People paid their taxes by working for the state.
Rows of stone storehouses held food for hard times.
The Inca made flat steps in the hills to grow crops.
Inca builders fitted huge stones together with no gaps between them.
Machu Picchu is a stone city high in the clouds.
A poor people called the Mexica came to a valley of lakes.
A story says they found an eagle sitting on a cactus.
Workers built long roads across the lake to reach the city.
In 1519, Tenochtitlan was larger than most cities in Europe.
Farmers made small gardens in the lake and grew food there.
The great market of Tlatelolco was crowded with buyers and sellers.
In 1428, three cities joined together in an alliance.
Many boys in Mexico went to school and learned from teachers.
A huge round stone shows how the Mexica thought about time.
At the Great Temple, priests offered gifts to their gods.
Long ago, people in Louisiana built a ring of earth mounds.
At Poverty Point, people made huge half circles of earth.
In Ohio, people built great circles and squares of earth.
The big earth rings in Ohio line up with the moon.
Hopewell traders exchanged copper, shells and sparkling stones across the continent.
Cahokia was a big city near the Mississippi River.
Monks Mound at Cahokia is the biggest earth mound in America.
At Cahokia, a circle of posts showed where the sun rose.
At Cahokia, one person was buried with thousands of shell beads.
By 1350, people had left Cahokia, long before Columbus came.
In the dry Southwest, farmers grew corn with very little rain.
In Chaco Canyon, people built a huge stone house with hundreds of rooms.
Chaco builders lined up their buildings with the sun and moon.
Wide straight roads ran for many miles out from Chaco.
Chaco people traded for bright feathers from far away.
Around 1150, a long drought led people to leave Chaco.
At Mesa Verde, people built homes inside the cliffs.
After a great drought, the cliff villages were left empty.
In Arizona, the Hohokam dug canals to bring river water to farms.
Taos Pueblo has been home to people for a thousand years.
In the eastern forests, people lived in villages and farmed corn.
The Haudenosaunee lived in long houses covered with bark.
Among the Haudenosaunee, women had a great deal of power.
A story tells how a Peacemaker ended long wars between nations.
The Great Law of Peace set up a council of chiefs.
People made belts from shell beads to help them remember laws.
Council meetings began with thanks to the Earth, rivers and trees.
Many peoples lit small fires to keep the forests open.
People in canoes gathered wild rice from lakes and rivers.
A Spanish explorer marched through large towns in the Southeast.
On the Pacific coast, huge runs of salmon fed many people.
Cedar trees gave people wood for houses, canoes and clothes.
Tall carved poles told the stories and honours of a family.
At a great feast called a potlatch, hosts gave gifts to their guests.
Inuit ancestors travelled across the cold Arctic about a thousand years ago.
Inuit hunters made kayaks from animal skin stretched over a frame.
A hunter waits for hours beside a hole in the ice.
Long ago, many villages stood along the rivers of the Amazon.
Amazon farmers made dark, rich soil that is still good today.
Many trees in the Amazon were planted by people long ago.
Norse sailors reached Newfoundland about five hundred years before Columbus.
The Norse stayed only a few years and then went home.
Columbus believed that he could sail west to reach Asia.
Three small ships left Spain in August 1492.
In October 1492, Columbus landed on an island in the Bahamas.
The Taino lived in villages, farmed cassava and travelled by canoe.
The islanders gave gifts, but Columbus soon asked about gold.
In 1493, Columbus came back with seventeen ships and many settlers.
The newcomers carried diseases that the Americas had never seen.
On Hispaniola, many of the Taino died in a few years.
In 1519, Cortes landed in Mexico with about five hundred men.
In November 1519, Moctezuma welcomed Cortes to Tenochtitlan.
In 1520, fighting broke out, and the Spanish had to flee.
In 1521, Cortes and his allies attacked Tenochtitlan again.
In 1532, a Spanish soldier named Pizarro captured Atahualpa.
The Inca fought on from a hidden mountain town.
Many people died, and forests grew back over empty fields.
New tools are teaching us more about the old Americas.
Today, many millions of people are descended from those first peoples.
The story of the Americas did not begin with Columbus.
B1B2: When Columbus sailed across the Atlantic in 1492, the Americas were not an empty land. Tens of millions of people already lived there, and scholars still argue about the exact number.
North America and South America are joined by a narrow strip of land in Central America. Together they stretch from the frozen Arctic to windy islands near the bottom of the world.
There was no single way of life in the Americas. Some peoples were farmers, some lived by fishing or hunting, and some built cities with thousands of homes.
Across the two continents, people spoke hundreds of languages. Many of them belonged to families that were not related to each other, so they were as different as English is from Chinese.

Columbus believed he had reached the Indies, near Asia, and that mistake gave Europe the word Indian. Today many people prefer Indigenous, Native American, or the name that each people uses for itself.
Scholars have given very different estimates for the people of the Americas in 1491. Some say a few million, and others say more than fifty million, so the true number is still unknown.
Archaeologists learn about the past by digging carefully in the ground. They find broken pots, stone tools, bones and the remains of houses, and each find is a small clue.

Other clues come from oral histories, which families have passed down for generations. A few Indigenous books also survive, and Spanish writers described what they saw, though they often misunderstood it.
Many Europeans later imagined the Americas as an untouched wilderness. In fact, people had been farming, burning, planting and building there for thousands of years.
To understand the world of 1491, we must go back much further in time. Our story begins with the first people who ever set foot on these continents.
About twenty thousand years ago, huge sheets of ice covered much of the north. Because so much water was frozen, the sea was more than a hundred metres lower than it is today.
Scientists call this lost land Beringia, and it was hundreds of miles wide. It was a cold, dry grassland where mammoths, horses and bison found enough to eat.
Some scientists think that the ancestors of Native Americans stayed in Beringia for thousands of years. Evidence from DNA suggests that they lived apart from other peoples until they moved south.

Two giant ice sheets covered much of Canada, and the way between them was probably blocked. A route inland may have opened only after about fourteen thousand years ago, which could be too late for the very first people.

Some scientists suggest that the first Americans travelled by boat along the Pacific coast. The cold water there was rich in kelp forests, fish, seals, shellfish and seabirds, so food was easy to find.

People certainly knew how to build boats, because they reached the Channel Islands off California about thirteen thousand years ago. Those islands were never joined to the mainland, so the travellers had to cross open water.

At White Sands in New Mexico, researchers found human footprints pressed into the mud of an ancient lake. Dating them in different ways suggests they are between twenty-one thousand and twenty-three thousand years old, although a few scientists still have doubts.

At Monte Verde in southern Chile, a camp was buried in wet peat that kept wood, hide and plants from rotting. The site is about fourteen and a half thousand years old, and it lies thousands of miles from Beringia.

Beautiful spear points were first found near Clovis, New Mexico, and they are about thirteen thousand years old. For many years experts believed the Clovis hunters were the first Americans, but older sites have shown that this was wrong.

In Montana, scientists studied the DNA of a small child who died about twelve thousand eight hundred years ago. His family line connects to many Native peoples across the Americas, which shows that they share very old ancestors.
The Americas of the ice age were full of giant animals. Mammoths and mastodons roamed the land, giant sloths browsed in the trees, and beavers grew as big as bears.
The hunters made spears with sharp tips of stone. They also used an atlatl, a short stick with a hook that let them throw a spear much farther and faster than by hand.

Between about thirteen thousand and ten thousand years ago, most of the giant animals of the Americas died out. Scientists still argue about why, and they point to hunting, a warming climate, or both.
As the ice melted, the sea rose again and forests spread across the land that had been covered in snow. Peoples had to learn new foods, new tools and new ways of living.
In 1927, a spear point was found among the bones of an extinct kind of bison near Folsom, New Mexico. It showed that people had lived in America at the same time as the ice age animals.
On the Great Plains, hunters worked together to drive herds of bison over cliffs. Some of these buffalo jumps, such as Head-Smashed-In in Alberta, were used for thousands of years.
Acorns are bitter, but Californian peoples learned to wash out the bitter taste and grind the nuts into meal. This food was so plentiful that many people lived there without farming.

Peoples who lived by the sea ate huge numbers of shellfish and piled the empty shells in heaps. Along the coast of Brazil, some of these shell mounds are taller than a house and thousands of years old.
In the dry lands of the West, people collected seeds, pine nuts and small animals, and moved with the seasons. Their baskets were woven so tightly, and sealed with pitch, that some could hold water.
By about ten thousand years ago, people lived in almost every part of the two continents. As groups settled in different places, their languages slowly grew apart.
The wild grass called teosinte grows in the hills of Mexico. It has a thin stalk and only a handful of seeds, each locked in a shell so hard that it is difficult to eat.
DNA studies point to the Balsas River valley in southern Mexico as the place where maize began. Gatherers there began to plant and tend teosinte about nine thousand years ago.
The oldest cobs that archaeologists have found are no longer than a thumb. Farmers saved seed from the best plants year after year, and over thousands of years the cobs grew larger.
American farmers did not make just one kind of corn. They grew blue, red, yellow, white and speckled kinds, and each one suited its own soil and climate.
Mexican cooks soaked corn in water mixed with lime or wood ash, a process called nixtamalization. The corn became softer, tastier and easier to grind into dough for tortillas and tamales.
Farmers also grew beans, which were first cultivated in both Mexico and the Andes. A meal of corn and beans gives the body more of what it needs than either food does alone.
Many peoples planted corn, beans and squash together and called them the Three Sisters. The beans climbed the corn, and the big squash leaves shaded the ground and kept weeds away.
Corn slowly travelled out from Mexico, both north and south. It reached the Andes thousands of years ago and the Southwest about four thousand years ago, but came to eastern North America much later.
In the dry lands of Arizona, Hopi farmers planted corn deep in the sand, where the earth still held some moisture. They grew good harvests in a place that gets very little rain.

Today farmers around the world harvest more than a billion tonnes of corn every year. In many Indigenous traditions it is also a sacred plant, and the Maya book Popol Vuh says that people were made from maize.
Wild potatoes are small, bitter and often poisonous to eat. Farmers near Lake Titicaca in the Andes learned to choose the safest ones, and they began to grow potatoes about eight thousand years ago.

Today the Andes still hold thousands of kinds of potato, in purple, red, yellow and even spotted skins. Farmers planted different kinds at different heights, from warm valleys to cold mountain fields.
Andean families spread potatoes on the ground to freeze at night and dry in the sun by day. They trampled out the water, and the result, called chuno, could be stored for years.
Quinoa is a small seed that grows well in the cold, thin air of the high Andes. It is rich in protein, and farmers there have grown it for thousands of years.
Tomatoes were grown in Mexico long before Europeans saw one, and our word tomato comes from the Nahuatl word tomatl. Before the 1500s, nobody in Italy had ever eaten a tomato.
People in the Americas have eaten chillies for thousands of years. After 1492 they spread around the world, so the hot food of India, Thailand and Sichuan in China is a fairly recent idea.
Chocolate is made from the seeds of the cacao tree, which first grew wild in the upper Amazon. Scientists have found traces of cacao in pots from Ecuador that are about 5,300 years old.
In Mesoamerica, chocolate was a drink, and it had no sugar. Cooks ground the beans, added water, maize and chilli, and poured the liquid between jars until it was frothy.

Farmers in the warm lowlands of South America grew cassava, a starchy root, and peanuts. Cassava is still a main food for hundreds of millions of people, though many of them live far away in Africa and Asia.
Farmers in the Americas grew many foods that people in other lands had never seen. Before 1492, nobody in Ireland ate potatoes, and nobody in Italy ate tomatoes.
Llamas were first kept by people in the Andes about six thousand years ago. A strong llama can carry about as much as a heavy backpack, so long lines of them travelled along the mountain paths.
Alpacas, a smaller cousin of the llama, were bred for their soft and warm wool. The wild vicuna gave an even finer wool, and in the Inca empire that cloth was kept for the ruler and his family.
Horses first appeared in the Americas millions of years ago, but they died out about ten thousand years ago. The Spanish brought horses back across the ocean in 1493.
There were no cattle, sheep, pigs or donkeys to carry the heavy loads. Men and women carried goods on their backs, often held by a strap across the forehead.
Archaeologists have found small clay animals with wheels in Mexico. People understood the idea of the wheel, but without animals to pull carts, it was not very useful for work.
Dogs travelled with early Americans and became hunters, guards and friends. The Coast Salish people of the Pacific Northwest even kept a woolly dog, and wove its soft hair into blankets.
Turkeys were first raised in Mexico, and later farmers in the Southwest kept them too. The Pueblo peoples made warm blankets by tying turkey feathers onto long cords of yucca.
Andean families raised guinea pigs, which they called cuy, for thousands of years. The animals lived inside the house, ate scraps, and were cooked for special feasts.

Without horses or carts, many peoples travelled by water instead. They built dugout canoes, light birchbark canoes in the northeast, reed boats on Lake Titicaca, and balsa rafts that sailed the Pacific coast.

Traders carried shells, blue turquoise, black volcanic glass called obsidian, and bright feathers across great distances. Volcanic glass from the Rocky Mountains has been found in Ohio, more than a thousand miles away.
In the dry Supe valley of Peru stand the ruins of Caral. This city is about five thousand years old, which makes it as old as the first cities of Egypt.
The people of Caral built six large platform mounds with steps, and a sunken round plaza for gatherings. They made no pottery, and archaeologists have found no sign of writing.

Inland farmers grew cotton, squash and beans, while fishers on the coast netted small fish such as anchovies and sardines. Scholars think the two groups traded, because fishers needed cotton for their nets.

Archaeologists found thirty-two flutes at Caral, made from the hollow bones of pelicans and other birds. Some of them are carved with the figures of birds and monkeys, so music clearly mattered in the city.

In the mountains of Peru, the people of Chavin de Huantar built a stone temple about three thousand years ago. Pilgrims from all over the Andes travelled there to see its carvings and to take part in rituals.

The Paracas people lived on the dry southern coast of Peru about two thousand years ago. They wrapped their dead in beautiful embroidered cloth, and the dry sand has kept the colours bright to this day.

On the desert of southern Peru, the Nazca people drew huge pictures of a hummingbird, a monkey, a spider and many other shapes. They made them by moving dark stones aside to show the pale ground beneath.
The Nazca also solved the problem of finding water in a desert. They dug channels under the ground, called puquios, and some of them are still used by farmers today.
The Moche lived on the north coast of Peru from about the year 100 to about 700. They built huge pyramids of mud bricks and long irrigation canals, and made pots shaped like people's faces.
In 1987, the archaeologist Walter Alva found the tomb of a Moche ruler at Sipan, in northern Peru. It was full of gold, turquoise and copper, because thieves had not found it.
The Olmec lived on the hot, wet coast of the Gulf of Mexico from about 3,200 to 2,400 years ago. Their name comes from a Nahuatl word that means rubber people.
The Olmec are famous for their colossal stone heads, and seventeen of them are known today. Each head was carved from one block of hard volcanic rock called basalt, and some are three metres tall.

The basalt came from the Tuxtla mountains, about eighty kilometres from San Lorenzo. Without wheels or animals, the workers probably used ropes, logs and rafts on the rivers, but nobody knows exactly how they did it.
Most scholars believe that each stone head shows a real ruler of the Olmec. Only a leader with great power could make hundreds of workers carve and move such heavy stones.
People in Mexico cut the rubber tree and collected its milky sap. They mixed it with the juice of a vine, and the result was a strong rubber that could bounce.
The Olmec and later peoples played a ballgame in courts shaped like the letter I. Players hit a heavy rubber ball with their hips, and they wore padding to avoid serious bruises.
Olmec artists also made small figures of green jade, a hard and precious stone. Many have round, baby-like faces and a mouth that looks like a jaguar's, and these shapes were copied by later peoples.
In 1999, a slab covered in sixty-two signs was found at Cascajal, in the Olmec lands. Some scholars think it is the oldest writing in the Americas, but others are not so sure.
About two and a half thousand years ago, the Zapotec built Monte Alban on a mountaintop in Oaxaca. They flattened the summit to make room for plazas, temples and tombs.
Mexico and Central America formed a region that scholars call Mesoamerica. Its many peoples spoke different languages, but they shared maize, ballgames, calendars, and the habit of building pyramids.
The Maya lived in what is now southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and parts of Honduras. They were never one empire, but dozens of city-states that each had its own king.
More than two thousand years ago, the Maya built El Mirador in the jungle of Guatemala. Its largest pyramid, La Danta, is one of the biggest ever built anywhere in the world.
Tikal in Guatemala was one of the greatest cities of the Maya. Its steep temples rose above the trees, and the tallest of them, Temple IV, is about seventy metres high.
Each Maya king led his city in religious ceremonies and in war. Tikal and Calakmul were the strongest cities, and each of them had allies that fought on its side.
At Palenque in Mexico, King Pakal ruled for sixty-eight years, from 615 to 683. In 1952, a team found his tomb at the bottom of a hidden stairway inside a pyramid.

Women sometimes ruled Maya cities as queens, and some ruled for many years. Lady Yohl Iknal governed Palenque from the year 583, and Lady Six Sky helped to rule the city of Naranjo more than a hundred years later.
The Maya lowlands have few rivers, and the dry season can be long. Maya engineers built reservoirs to store rainwater, and people also used deep natural pools in the limestone called cenotes.
Most Maya people were farmers and craftworkers rather than nobles or kings. They grew maize, beans and squash, lived in simple houses of poles and thatch, and walked into the city on market days.
At Bonampak in southern Mexico, the walls of a small building are covered with bright paintings from about the year 790. They show a royal court, musicians in masks, and a battle.
Maya potters painted bowls and tall cups with scenes of gods, kings and animals. Some artists were so proud of their work that they signed their names on it.
The Maya wrote in hieroglyphs, small square signs made of pictures. Some signs stood for whole words, and others stood for sounds, so a scribe could write almost anything in the Maya language.

For many years, nobody could read the Maya signs. In the twentieth century, scholars such as Yuri Knorozov and Tatiana Proskouriakoff showed that the signs recorded sounds and the real lives of kings.
The Maya also wrote books on folded sheets of bark paper. In 1562 a Spanish friar named Diego de Landa burned many of them, and only four survive today.
At Copan, in what is now Honduras, a temple has a great staircase of sixty-three steps. About 2,200 signs are carved on it, and it is the longest Maya text that survives.
The Maya counted in twenties, using a dot for one and a bar for five. They also had a sign for zero, shaped like a shell, which made it possible to write very large numbers.
The Maya kept a sacred calendar of 260 days and a solar year of 365 days. The two ran together like cogwheels, and they met again only after fifty-two years.
Maya astronomers watched the planet Venus and worked out that it returns every 584 days. They also made tables for predicting eclipses, and they wrote them in their books.
Some people claimed that the Maya predicted the end of the world in December 2012. In fact, the Long Count simply finished one great cycle, like a car odometer turning over, and started another.
A scribe was an important person in a Maya city. Many came from noble families, and some were even princes who wrote and painted for the king.
The Popol Vuh is a Maya book of stories, written down in the 1500s by Maya authors. It tells how the Hero Twins played the ballgame against the Lords of Death and won.

Teotihuacan, near modern Mexico City, was laid out on a grid, like a modern city. Around the year 500, it may have held more than a hundred thousand people, which made it one of the largest cities in the world.
The main street of Teotihuacan was a wide road more than two kilometres long, which the Aztecs called the Avenue of the Dead. Temples, palaces and pyramids stood on both sides of it.
The Pyramid of the Sun, about sixty-five metres high, is one of the biggest buildings of the ancient Americas. Beside the avenue stands the smaller Pyramid of the Moon, set in front of a mountain.
In 2003, archaeologists discovered a long tunnel under the Temple of the Feathered Serpent. At the end they found hundreds of offerings, including shells, jade, and little sculptures.
Most people in Teotihuacan lived in walled compounds, which were like apartment blocks with rooms around courtyards. The walls were covered with white plaster and often painted with bright murals.
Maya inscriptions record that a lord called Siyaj Kak arrived at Tikal in the year 378. Many scholars think he came from Teotihuacan, because the new kings used its symbols.
Around the year 550, fire destroyed many of the temples and palaces at the centre of Teotihuacan. Scholars still argue about why, and they point to a rebellion, a drought, or both.

Between about 800 and 900, many Maya cities in the southern lowlands stopped building monuments and slowly emptied. Records in cave stalagmites show that there were long droughts, and wars were also common.
As the southern cities faded, Chichen Itza in the north of the Yucatan grew rich. Its great pyramid, El Castillo, has 365 steps, one for each day of the year, and a huge ball court lies beside it.
The Maya people did not vanish when the old cities were abandoned. Millions of their descendants live today in Mexico, Guatemala and Belize, and many of them speak a Mayan language at home.

The Andes are one of the highest mountain chains on Earth, and many peoples had lived there before the Inca. Tiwanaku, near Lake Titicaca, and Wari, in Peru, were powerful states between about 500 and 1000.

On the north coast of Peru, the Chimu kingdom built Chan Chan, the largest mud-brick city in the Americas. The walls were decorated with fish, birds and waves, and about thirty thousand people lived there.
The Inca began as a small group in the valley of Cusco, high in the Andes. Their own stories say that the first Inca, Manco Capac, came from the region of Lake Titicaca.
According to Inca tradition, a rival people called the Chanka attacked Cusco about 1438. The young prince Pachacuti led the defence and won, and afterwards he began to build an empire.
Pachacuti, his son Topa Inca and his grandson Huayna Capac built an empire called Tawantinsuyu, which means the four parts together. It ran for about four thousand kilometres along the Andes.

The Inca did not rely only on their armies to win loyalty. They gave gifts to local lords, moved families from one region to another, and taught the Quechua language so that everyone could talk together.
The ruler was called the Sapa Inca, and people believed that he was the Son of the Sun. When a ruler died, his body was preserved as a mummy and was still treated as a member of the court.
The Inca honoured Inti, the Sun, as their chief god. They also honoured Viracocha, the creator, and Pachamama, the Earth Mother, and the temple of the Sun in Cusco was rich with gold.
Every year at the winter solstice, in June, the Inca held a great festival for the Sun, called Inti Raymi. People still hold a celebration with that name in Cusco today.
For the Inca, fine cloth was as precious as gold. Skilled weavers made it from the wool of alpacas and vicunas, and rulers gave it as a gift to reward loyal people.
The Inca built more than thirty thousand kilometres of roads, which climbed mountains and crossed deserts and forests. Some roads were paved with stone and had steps, walls and drains.
Inca engineers wove grass into thick ropes and hung long bridges across deep river gorges. At Q'eswachaka in Peru, local people still rebuild one such bridge every June, using the old methods.
Messages travelled along the roads with relay runners called chasqui. They waited at small huts every few kilometres, and each runner passed the message on to the next one.
Along the main roads, the Inca built roadside stations called tambos, about a day's walk apart. Officials, messengers and armies could rest there, and find food and warm blankets.
The Inca did not write, but they used the quipu, a set of cords tied with knots. The position of each knot stood for ones, tens or hundreds, so officials could record numbers.
The Inca had no money, so people paid their taxes with their own work. This system was called the mita, and the state fed the workers and held feasts for them in return.
The Inca built thousands of stone storehouses on hillsides, where cool winds kept food fresh. They held maize, chuno, cloth and tools, and they helped people survive in years of bad harvests.
The Inca built terraces, which are flat steps cut into steep slopes and held up by stone walls. Water ran down through them, and some terraces at Moray are built in great circles.
Inca stonemasons cut huge stones so exactly that they fit together without any mortar. Their walls have survived centuries of earthquakes, while many Spanish buildings in the same region have fallen.
Machu Picchu was built about 1450, probably as a country estate for the ruler Pachacuti. It sits on a ridge about 2,400 metres above sea level, and the outside world learned of it in 1911.
The Mexica, whom Europeans later called Aztecs, came to the Valley of Mexico in the 1200s. Their own stories say that they had walked a long way from a place called Aztlan.
According to their story, the Mexica were told to settle where they saw an eagle on a cactus. They found it on a marshy island in Lake Texcoco and founded Tenochtitlan there, about 1325.

The Mexica built long stone causeways across the lake, so that people could walk to the island from the shore. They also made dikes to hold back the salty water, and an aqueduct that brought fresh water into the city.

By 1519, Tenochtitlan may have held two hundred thousand people, which was more than almost any city in Europe. A Spanish soldier named Bernal Diaz wrote that some of his friends wondered if they were dreaming.
The Mexica made chinampas, which are narrow garden plots built up from mud and plants in the shallow lake. The soil was so rich and wet that farmers could harvest several crops in a year.
The market of Tlatelolco, beside Tenochtitlan, was the biggest that the Spanish had ever seen. Cortes said that sixty thousand people came each day, and traders used cacao beans as small change.
In 1428, Tenochtitlan joined with Texcoco and Tlacopan to form the Triple Alliance. Together they conquered many neighbours and demanded tribute, which was a regular payment of goods.
Many boys in Mexico went to school when they were in their teens. Ordinary boys learned to fight and to serve the city, while the sons of nobles went to a school for leaders and priests.
The Stone of the Sun is a huge carved disk about three and a half metres wide. It shows the Aztec ideas about time and the world, and it was found beneath Mexico City in 1790.

The Templo Mayor, or Great Temple, stood at the centre of Tenochtitlan. The Aztecs practised human sacrifice, which their gods were believed to need, though Spanish writers sometimes exaggerated how many people died.
At Watson Brake in Louisiana, people built a ring of earth mounds about five thousand years ago. They were hunters and gatherers, not farmers, and the site is one of the oldest of its kind.
Poverty Point, also in Louisiana, is about 3,400 years old. Its people built six huge half-circles of earth, with a plaza in the middle, and they brought stone from far away.
About two thousand years ago, the Hopewell peoples of the Ohio valley built great earth circles, squares and octagons. Some of these shapes were nearly a kilometre across.

The Octagon at Newark in Ohio lines up with the rising of the moon, in a cycle that lasts a little more than eighteen years. In 2023, the Hopewell earthworks became a World Heritage Site, which means that the world now protects them.

The Hopewell peoples gathered precious materials from all over the continent. They collected copper from Lake Superior, shells from the Gulf of Mexico, mica from the Appalachian hills and obsidian from the Rocky Mountains.
Cahokia grew very quickly after about the year 1050, beside the Mississippi River in Illinois. At its height, it was the largest city north of Mexico, with at least ten thousand people.
Monks Mound at Cahokia is the largest earth mound in the Americas, about thirty metres high. Workers built it in stages from baskets of soil, and a large building stood on top.
