Near the great mound, the people of Cahokia raised circles of tall wooden posts, which archaeologists call Woodhenge. The sun rose between particular posts on important days of the year, marking the seasons.
In Mound 72 at Cahokia, archaeologists found a man buried on a bed of shell beads shaped like a bird. Many other people lay near him, which suggests that some of them were sacrificed.
By about 1350, Cahokia was almost empty, long before any European came near. Scholars suggest that floods, drought, war and a lack of wood for fuel and building may all have played a part.
The Ancestral Pueblo peoples lived in the dry canyons and mesas of the American Southwest. They grew corn, beans and squash, and they knew how to save every drop of rain.
In Chaco Canyon, in New Mexico, people built a vast stone building called Pueblo Bonito. They added to it over three hundred years, from about 850 to 1150, until it had hundreds of rooms.
The builders of Chaco paid great attention to the sun and the moon. On Fajada Butte, a thin beam of light once crossed a carved spiral at midsummer, and it is called the Sun Dagger.
Straight roads, about nine metres wide, ran out from Chaco Canyon across the desert for many miles. They were made by hand, since the people had no wheels, horses or carts.

Chaco was linked to many distant places by trade. Archaeologists found macaw skeletons from Mexico, traces of chocolate in jars, and tens of thousands of wooden beams carried from mountains many miles away.
Around the year 1150, a long drought hit the Southwest. The people of Chaco slowly moved away to other places, though Chaco has remained a sacred place for their descendants.
At Mesa Verde in Colorado, people built whole villages inside shelves of the cliffs, from about the year 1190. The largest, Cliff Palace, has about a hundred and fifty rooms and twenty-three kivas.
Between 1276 and 1299 a severe drought hit the region, and the cliff villages were gradually left. The people moved south to the Rio Grande and to other places with more water.
In the hot desert of southern Arizona, the Hohokam people dug hundreds of miles of canals. They carried river water to their fields, and the modern city of Phoenix uses some of the same routes.
Taos Pueblo in New Mexico has been lived in for about a thousand years. Families there still live in earthen houses and still replaster the walls each year, and it is a World Heritage Site.
The Eastern Woodlands stretch from the Great Lakes to the Atlantic coast and south to the Gulf of Mexico. Peoples such as the Haudenosaunee, Cherokee and Wampanoag farmed, fished and hunted there.
The Haudenosaunee, whose name means People of the Longhouse, lived in long houses with frames of poles and walls of bark. Some were more than thirty metres long and held many related families.

Haudenosaunee families traced their descent through the mother, not the father. Women looked after the farm fields, and the senior women of each clan, the clan mothers, chose the chiefs and could remove them.
According to oral tradition, the five nations were at war until a man called the Peacemaker came and taught them a new way. His helper was Hiawatha, and estimates of the date vary a great deal.
The Great Law of Peace created a council of fifty chiefs from the five nations. It also gave the world a symbol, the Tree of Peace, a white pine under whose roots the weapons were buried.
Wampum are strings and belts of small beads cut from purple and white shells. The patterns recorded promises, laws and treaties, and they helped the speakers to remember them.

Haudenosaunee meetings began with a Thanksgiving Address, in which speakers gave thanks to the rivers, the plants, the animals, the sun and the moon. Leaders then talked at length until they reached agreement.
Many peoples in the east burned the undergrowth of their forests on purpose each year. The fires made the woods open and park-like, and they helped nut trees, berries and deer to flourish.
In the northern lakes, peoples such as the Ojibwe harvested wild rice from canoes, knocking the grains into the boat with sticks. On the prairies, people burned the grass to keep it fresh for bison.
Between 1539 and 1543, the Spanish explorer Hernando de Soto marched through the Southeast. His men described large towns and well-planted fields, but a century later many of those towns were gone.
Along the Pacific coast, from Alaska to Oregon, millions of salmon swam up the rivers every year. The peoples there became rich and powerful by fishing and gathering, and did not need to farm.

The cedar tree gave these peoples nearly everything that they needed for daily life. They split planks from living trees for houses, carved canoes up to twenty metres long, and wove the inner bark into baskets.
Totem poles were carved from huge cedar trunks, and they were covered with figures of ravens, eagles, bears and whales. The figures were family crests, which told stories and honoured people.
A potlatch was a great feast at which a family gave gifts to its guests. The guests acted as witnesses to a marriage, a naming or a change of rank, and the more the host gave, the greater his honour.
About a thousand years ago, the ancestors of the Inuit began to travel east from Alaska. In a few hundred years, they had spread across the Arctic coast of Canada as far as Greenland.
An Inuit kayak had a light frame of wood or whalebone, covered with sealskin that had been sewn to keep the water out. The hunter sat inside and moved quietly over the water to approach seals.

In the winter, Inuit hunters waited patiently beside holes in the sea ice for seals to come up to breathe. They also found their way across the snow by reading the wind, the stars and the shapes of the drifts.

The Amazon rainforest was not empty before the year 1492, as people once believed. In the Upper Xingu in Brazil, villages with plazas were joined by wide roads, and people farmed cassava and fished in the rivers.
Most Amazon soil is poor, but in some places the earth is dark, deep and fertile. Scientists call it terra preta, and it was made by people from charcoal, broken pots, bones and food waste.

In the southwestern Amazon, scientists found huge earthworks of squares and circles that were built many centuries ago. Many useful trees, such as Brazil nut trees, grow most thickly near old settlements.

About the year 1000, Norse sailors from Greenland reached Newfoundland, in what is now Canada. They built turf houses at a place called L'Anse aux Meadows, and tree rings suggest that they were still there in 1021.
The Norse sagas tell of fights with the local people, whom they called Skraelings. The settlers stayed only a few years and went home, and the two worlds were left apart for another five centuries.

Christopher Columbus, a sailor from Genoa in Italy, believed he could reach Asia by sailing west. He thought the earth was smaller than it really is, and he did not know that two continents lay in the way.
Columbus sailed from Spain in August 1492 with three small ships, the Nina, the Pinta and the Santa Maria. After a stop in the Canary Islands, the crew sailed west for more than a month.
On the twelfth of October 1492, Columbus landed on an island in the Bahamas. Its people, the Taino, called it Guanahani, and Columbus gave it the Spanish name San Salvador.
The Taino lived in villages led by chiefs called caciques. They farmed cassava and maize, slept in hammocks, and travelled the sea in canoes, and these words came into English from their language.

Columbus wrote that the islanders were generous and gentle, and they gave the strangers food, cotton and parrots. But he soon began asking where he could find gold, and he took some people away by force.
Columbus returned to Spain with news of his discovery, and in 1493 he sailed back with seventeen ships. The ships carried more than a thousand men, together with horses, cattle, pigs and seeds.
The Europeans carried diseases such as smallpox, measles and influenza, which had never reached the Americas. The people there had no protection, and these illnesses killed huge numbers of them.

On the island of Hispaniola, the Taino population fell very sharply within a few decades. Scholars disagree about how many people lived there at first, but the causes were disease, forced labour and violence.
In 1519, Hernan Cortes landed on the coast of Mexico with about five hundred soldiers. A woman named Malinche translated for him, and many peoples who disliked Mexica rule joined his side.

In November 1519, the Mexica ruler Moctezuma met Cortes on the great causeway and welcomed the Spanish into his city. Within a few days, however, Cortes had taken the ruler prisoner in his own palace.
In 1520, fighting broke out in Tenochtitlan, and Moctezuma died in the confusion. The Spanish fled in the night, losing many men, but then smallpox spread through the city and killed thousands.
In 1521, Cortes returned with tens of thousands of Indigenous allies and built boats to attack the island city. After a siege of about seventy-five days, Tenochtitlan fell in August.
In 1532, Francisco Pizarro and fewer than two hundred men captured the Inca ruler Atahualpa at Cajamarca. The Inca empire had just come out of a civil war, and disease had already weakened it.

Some Inca leaders refused to give up, and they fought on from a hidden mountain stronghold called Vilcabamba. The last of them was captured in 1572, but Inca culture and language survived in the Andes.

In the worst-hit regions, most people died within about a hundred years, though nobody knows exactly how many. Some scientists think that forests growing on empty fields may have cooled the climate, but others doubt it.

Today lidar, a laser survey from the air, can see through the trees. In 2018 it showed more than sixty thousand Maya buildings in Guatemala, and DNA studies and tree rings are also adding to the story.
The first peoples of the Americas did not disappear, and their descendants live in every country. Many millions still speak languages such as Quechua, Nahuatl, Guarani and the Mayan languages.
The story of the Americas did not begin in 1492, and it did not end then either. Every day, people around the world eat foods such as potatoes, maize, tomatoes and chocolate that first grew there.
C1C2: In the year before Columbus set sail, the Americas were home to tens of millions of people who spoke hundreds of languages and lived in very different kinds of societies. Scholars still argue about the exact numbers, because the evidence is scattered and the later collapse of so many peoples makes counting difficult. This is the story of those peoples and of the world they had built over many thousands of years.

The Americas form a vast chain of land that begins in the frozen Arctic, passes through deserts, prairies and rainforests, and ends in the windy islands near the southern tip of South America. A narrow neck of land in Central America, which is called an isthmus, joins the two continents together into one long chain. Within that enormous space lay almost every kind of climate and landscape that the planet has to offer, and people had made a home in nearly all of them.

It would be a mistake to picture a single Native American way of life, for the peoples of the Americas were as different from one another as the peoples of Europe, Africa and Asia. Some followed herds across the open plains, while others fished the cold northern rivers or tended terraced fields on steep mountainsides. Still others governed great cities with busy markets, tall temples and officials who collected taxes from the people.

The Americas held an astonishing variety of languages, and linguists have sorted them into dozens of families with no known relationship to one another. A speaker of Nahuatl in Mexico could no more understand a speaker of Navajo, or of Quechua in the Andes, than an English speaker could follow Japanese. Many of these languages are still spoken by living communities today, and some are now being taught again to children.

When Columbus landed in 1492 he believed that he had reached the Indies, the rich lands of eastern Asia, and the word Indian grew out of that mistake. The name stuck, but it covers hundreds of separate nations, which is why many people today prefer to say Indigenous or Native American, or better still to use the name that each people gives itself. In this book you will meet the Inuit, the Mohawk, the Maya, the Inca and many others, each in its own right.

Counting the people of the Americas before 1492 is one of the hardest problems in history, and estimates range from only a few million to well over fifty million. The difficulty is that very few records exist from before the great epidemics, and the early European counts were rough guesses. Most scholars now accept the higher figures more readily than they once did, though the debate is far from settled.

Much of what we know about the early Americas comes from archaeologists, who dig with great patience and record every object they find. A broken pot, a stone tool, a heap of shells or the dark stain of a vanished wall can each tell a story about the people who left it behind. Put together, such clues build a picture of lives that no one wrote down.

Archaeology is not the only guide, for many Indigenous peoples have preserved their own histories in spoken tradition, carefully handed down from one generation to the next. A small number of painted books also survived the conquest, and Spanish writers left long accounts of what they saw. Each source has limits, and good historians weigh them against one another instead of trusting any single voice.

The settlers who came after Columbus often described the Americas as a pristine wilderness, a world that nature had made and that no one had touched. This picture was largely wrong, because Indigenous peoples had spent thousands of years planting crops, burning grasslands, building towns and changing the course of rivers. Much of what looked like untouched nature was in fact the work of human hands.

To understand the world that Columbus found, we have to travel back thousands of years before him, long before the first stone was laid in any city. Our journey begins with the earliest travellers, who crossed an ancient frozen landscape toward a land that no human had ever seen. From the footsteps of those first travellers, everything else in this long and surprising story will slowly grow.

During the last ice age, enormous sheets of ice smothered much of northern Asia, Europe and North America, and the water they locked away lowered the level of the oceans by well over a hundred metres. Coastlines that we know today lay far out of the water, and the seabed became dry land. It was a very different map from the one that we find in our atlases today, and the people of that age walked across places that now lie under the sea.

The land that joined Siberia to Alaska is called Beringia, and it was no narrow bridge but a broad plain that stretched for hundreds of miles from north to south. Its cold grasses fed mammoths, horses and bison, and the hunters who followed those animals gradually found themselves living in a country of their own. Today almost all of that lost country lies beneath the cold waters of the Bering Sea, where it can be explored only with special equipment.

Studies of ancient and modern DNA hint that the ancestors of the first Americans may have lived in Beringia for many thousands of years, cut off from other peoples by mountains and ice. If this is right, they were already a distinct community, with their own habits and stories, long before they ever entered the Americas proper. The idea is still debated, as are so many scientific ideas about this distant period, and new evidence may yet change the story.

Across Canada lay two vast ice sheets, and the corridor between them seems to have been closed, or at least too bleak and barren to cross, for many thousands of years. Geologists think it opened up only about fourteen thousand years ago, and since there is good evidence that people were already living far to the south by then, the first travellers may have found another way. That discovery changed the whole conversation, because it made the sea route look more likely than the road through the ice.

One popular idea is that the earliest settlers followed the Pacific shoreline in small boats, and that the coastal kelp forests, which teem with fish, shellfish, seals and seabirds, served them as a kind of highway. Such a route would have offered food at every stop and a familiar way of life along the whole journey. The evidence lies mostly under the sea today, which makes the theory hard to prove.

There is firm evidence that early Americans were skilled sailors, for people were living on the Channel Islands off the coast of California about thirteen thousand years ago. Those islands were separated from the mainland by water even in the ice age, so the settlers must have crossed the sea in boats of wood, reed or hide. Such craft rot away quickly, which is why none from so long ago has ever been found by archaeologists.

In the desert of White Sands in New Mexico, the footprints of teenagers and children lie preserved in what was once the soft mud of a lake shore. Careful dating with seeds, pollen and other methods suggests that they were made between about twenty-one thousand and twenty-three thousand years ago, far earlier than many experts once thought possible. A few researchers remain cautious about the dates, so the conclusion is still being tested by other teams using different methods.

Monte Verde in southern Chile is one of the most important sites in the Americas, because the wet peat that covered it preserved wooden stakes, scraps of hide, seaweed and even the chewed remains of medicinal plants. Radiocarbon dating puts the camp at about fourteen and a half thousand years ago, which shows that people had already travelled the length of two continents. It also proved that the old story of a single late arrival was wrong.

In the 1930s, archaeologists near Clovis in New Mexico found elegant stone spear points with a shallow groove along each face, and similar points have since turned up across most of North America. For decades they were believed to belong to the very first Americans, but discoveries such as Monte Verde showed that people had arrived much earlier. The Clovis hunters are still admired for their remarkable craftsmanship, and modern flint workers still study them closely to learn how they were made.

At a site in Montana, the bones of a small child who died roughly twelve thousand eight hundred years ago were found buried with tools and spear points. When scientists read his DNA in 2014, they discovered that he was related to many Indigenous peoples in both North and South America, which shows how widely the early settlers had spread. Many Indigenous peoples also tell their own accounts of where they came from, and these are respected alongside the scientific evidence.

The newcomers entered a continent that was crowded with creatures far larger than any alive there today. Mammoths and mastodons trampled the grasslands, ground sloths as heavy as oxen pulled down branches, and short-faced bears and sabre-toothed cats hunted among them. It was a world of giants, and the first people had to learn how to live beside them.

Hunting a mammoth was dangerous work, and it demanded a great deal of skill, courage and careful teamwork. The hunters tipped their spears with razor-sharp stone points and launched them with an atlatl, a hooked wooden handle that worked like an extra length of arm and multiplied the power of the throw. The bow and arrow came much later, and did not spread across most of North America until about two thousand years ago, so the atlatl served for thousands of years.

Within the space of a few thousand years, mammoths, mastodons, giant sloths, native horses and many other large animals vanished from the Americas. Some scientists blame the hunters, others blame the rapid warming of the climate, and many now think that a combination of the two was responsible. It remains one of the great unsolved questions about the ancient continent, and the answer may differ from one animal to another.

When the ice age ended, about twelve thousand years ago, the glaciers drew back, the seas climbed steadily upward and forests advanced over ground that had been bare tundra. Every community had to adapt to a new landscape with different animals, plants and seasons. The ability to adapt, more than any single invention, is the secret of the first Americans' success.

Near the town of Folsom in New Mexico, a cowboy noticed a heap of strange bones in the early twentieth century, and in 1927 archaeologists found a stone spear point lying among the ribs of a bison from an extinct species. The discovery settled an old argument, because it proved that people had lived in America more than ten thousand years ago. Folsom points are now known to be more than twelve thousand years old, and the site is still studied by researchers today.

Without horses, the hunters of the Plains relied on cunning and cooperation, and they steered whole herds of bison between lines of stones toward the edge of a cliff. Some of these buffalo jumps, such as Head-Smashed-In in Alberta, were used again and again for thousands of years, and their layers of bone are many metres deep. The meat fed entire communities, while hides, bones and sinew became clothing, tools and shelter.

Acorns contain bitter chemicals, yet the peoples of California perfected a method of washing them with water until they were sweet enough to eat, and then ground them into a nourishing meal. Oak trees gave so generous a harvest that dense communities could live for thousands of years without planting a single field. California became one of the most crowded regions of North America, with dozens of different languages.

On many coasts, people lived largely on shellfish, fish and sea mammals, and over the centuries the discarded shells formed immense mounds that rose above the villages. The shell mounds of Brazil, known as sambaquis, can be as tall as a ten-storey building, and many of them contain burials, which suggests that they were sacred places as well as heaps of waste. They have lasted far longer than any wooden house could, and some of them are now protected as important monuments of the past.

In the deserts and dry mountains of the West, families moved with the seasons to harvest seeds, roots and pine nuts and to trap rabbits and other small game. Their knowledge of the land was astonishingly detailed, because survival depended on knowing exactly where water would be found and when each plant would ripen. Baskets woven from grasses and coated with pitch were so watertight that some could carry water across the desert.

By about ten thousand years ago, human beings had settled almost every habitable corner of the Americas, from the northern forests to the southern tip of Patagonia. As the groups made their homes in separate valleys, coasts and plains, their ways of speaking drifted apart, and over thousands of years a few original languages grew into hundreds. Each community developed deep knowledge of its own corner of the world, including its animals, its plants, its weather and its dangers.

Nothing about the plant called teosinte would suggest that it could ever feed a whole continent of people. This wild grass of southern Mexico has a thin, branching stalk and a few rows of tiny seeds, each locked inside a case so hard that it can survive the stomach of a cow. Yet it is the ancestor of corn, or maize, as most scientists call it, and the change between the two is one of the greatest feats of plant breeding.

Genetic studies suggest that the home of maize was the valley of the Balsas River in southern Mexico, where gatherers began to plant and tend the wild grass about nine thousand years ago. It may have been the sweet juice of the stalks, rather than the seeds, that first attracted them. Nobody can be sure, since the first farmers left no written record of their experiments.

The earliest cobs found in the caves of Mexico are tiny, with only a few small kernels, and they are not much longer than a human thumb. Generation after generation, farmers saved the seeds of the plants that bore the biggest and softest kernels and sowed them again in the next spring. This patient selection, repeated over thousands of years, slowly produced the corn that we recognise today.

Over the centuries, farmers bred dozens of kinds of maize, with kernels in blue, red, yellow, white, black and speckled colours, and with ears of every size from a finger to a forearm. Some varieties ripen quickly in short northern summers, while others thrive in thin mountain air or in parched desert soil. Such variety was a form of insurance, since a bad season rarely ruined every kind at once.

Long ago, Mexican cooks discovered that soaking dried corn in water mixed with lime or wood ash, a method now called nixtamalization, made the kernels easier to grind and the dough easier to shape. The treatment also released nutrients, including a vitamin called niacin, that the body cannot otherwise take from corn. When Europeans later grew maize without this step, some of the people who depended on it fell ill with a disease called pellagra.

Beans were domesticated independently in Mexico and in the Andes, and they became the faithful companion of the corn plant on both continents. Corn on its own lacks some of the building blocks that the body needs, but beans supply them, so a simple meal of tortillas and beans is far more nourishing than either food alone. Squash, which is even older as a crop than either of the other two, completed the partnership and added vitamins and oil to the meal.

In the fields of the Haudenosaunee and of many other peoples, the Three Sisters of corn, beans and squash were planted together in the same mound of earth. The cornstalk gave the bean vines something to climb, the beans enriched the soil with nitrogen, and the broad squash leaves shaded the ground and held back the weeds. In Mexico the same idea survives in the milpa, a field of mixed crops that families still cultivate today.

Maize spread slowly, moving from farmer to farmer and from valley to valley, as people traded seeds and shared knowledge. It reached the Andes thousands of years ago, arrived in the American Southwest about four thousand years ago, and did not become a staple food in the eastern woodlands until about a thousand years ago. Along the way, farmers kept adapting it to new places, so that the corn of the cold north became very different from the corn of the warm south.

In the dry canyons of northern Arizona, Hopi farmers planted their corn unusually deep, using long roots and the moisture hidden beneath the surface to raise a crop in a place that receives very little rain. Such skill came from generations of careful observation, and it was passed down in songs, rituals and family lessons. It still allows Hopi farmers to grow corn on land that seems far too dry.

Corn is now one of the most widely grown crops on Earth, with more than a billion tonnes harvested each year for food, animal feed and fuel. For many Indigenous peoples, however, it is much more than a crop, and the Maya book known as the Popol Vuh tells how the first people were formed from maize dough. A plant that began as a thin wild grass has become a gift to the whole world.

The wild ancestors of the potato contain bitter chemicals that can make a person very sick, which makes it all the more remarkable that anyone ever tried to eat them. Around the shores of Lake Titicaca in the Andes, patient farmers chose the mildest tubers, planted them, and over thousands of years produced a safe and nourishing crop. The first potato farmers began their patient work about eight thousand years ago, and their descendants still grow the crop in the same mountains today.

The potatoes of the Andes come in an extraordinary range of colours and shapes, including purple, pink, yellow and blue, round, knobbly and long and twisted. Farmers matched each kind to a particular height and soil, planting some in warm valleys and others in fields more than four thousand metres above the sea. Today, thousands of these native varieties are still grown in Peru and its neighbours.

High in the Andes, the nights are bitterly cold and the days are bright and dry, and farmers used those conditions to make chuno, a potato that lasts for years. They left the tubers to freeze overnight, trampled out the water with their feet, and let the sun dry what remained into hard, light lumps. A year of poor harvests could be survived on food that had been saved for just such a time.

Quinoa thrives where almost no other grain will grow, in the cold, dry, windy fields of the high Andes. It is rich in protein, and its tiny seeds can be boiled into porridge, ground into flour or fermented into drinks. Farmers have cultivated it for thousands of years, and it has recently become popular in kitchens far from South America.

The tomato was a Mexican crop, cultivated by the peoples of Mesoamerica and cooked into sauces that were ground in a stone bowl with chillies and salt. Our word for it comes from tomatl, in the Nahuatl language of the Mexica. It is a curious fact that Italian cooking, which seems so rooted in tomatoes, had none until they were carried across the Atlantic in the sixteenth century.

Chillies were among the first crops of the Americas, and farmers developed dozens of kinds, from sweet and mild to fiercely hot. Cooks used them to flavour food, to preserve it and to add some vitamin C to a diet. After the Spanish and Portuguese carried them across the oceans, chillies transformed the cooking of India, Thailand and western China, where no one had tasted a hot pepper before.

The cacao tree is native to the warm, wet forests of the upper Amazon, and its seeds were first used by people there in ancient times. In 2018, scientists reported finding traces of cacao in pottery from the Mayo-Chinchipe culture of Ecuador, which dates back about 5,300 years. From South America, the tree and its uses spread north to Central America and Mexico.

The first chocolate was not a sweet bar but a bitter, foaming drink that people in Mesoamerica prepared by grinding roasted cacao beans, mixing them with water, and sometimes adding chilli, vanilla or flowers. To raise the froth, a cook poured the liquid from one jar to another from a height, as Maya paintings on pottery show. The drink was valued so highly that kings, warriors and traders served it at feasts.

In the warm, wet lowlands of South America, farmers cultivated cassava, a starchy root that grows well in poor soil, and peanuts, which ripen underground. Cassava was prepared with care, because the bitter kinds contain poison that must be removed by grating, squeezing and cooking. The crop was carried across the oceans after 1492, and today it feeds hundreds of millions of people in Africa and Asia.

The list of American crops goes on, and includes avocados, pineapples, vanilla orchids, sunflowers grown in eastern North America about four thousand years ago, and a kind of cotton cultivated on the coast of Peru. In the world of 1491, no one in Ireland had eaten a potato, no one in Italy had eaten a tomato and no one in Switzerland had tasted chocolate. A great deal of what we think of as old and traditional European food began with American farmers.

High in the Andes, people tamed the llama about six thousand years ago, and it became the great pack animal of the western side of South America. A llama can carry a load of about twenty-five kilograms, and it can walk for days over rough ground on very little food and water. Long caravans of these patient animals linked farms, markets and cities across the mountains, and they are still used in some remote places today.

The alpaca was raised mainly for its wool, which is soft, warm and available in a wide range of natural colours from white to brown to black. The wild vicuna produces the finest fibre of all, and in the Inca empire cloth made from it was reserved for the ruler and the nobility. Llamas and alpacas also gave meat, and their dried dung made a useful fuel on treeless mountainsides.

The story of the horse began in North America, where its distant ancestors lived for millions of years, but the species disappeared from the continent at the end of the ice age. Because of this, no American people had ever ridden a horse or seen one before the Spanish brought horses from Europe on the second voyage of Columbus in 1493. Horses were to change the lives of many peoples in the centuries that followed.

In most of the Americas there were no oxen, donkeys or camels to bear the burden, so the heavy work of moving goods fell to people themselves. Porters carried loads on their backs, supported by a broad strap that passed across the forehead, and trained carriers could cover astonishing distances in a single day. Whole systems of trade and tax depended on the strength and endurance of such workers.

Among the most surprising discoveries in Mexico are small clay animals mounted on wheels, which children probably pulled along by a string. This proves that the idea of the wheel was known, yet nobody built wheeled carts for travel or work, perhaps because there were no large animals to pull them, and the land is so steep and rough. It was a matter of circumstances rather than of cleverness, and the same people were brilliant builders, farmers and astronomers.

The dog is the oldest animal companion of human beings in the Americas, and it came with the early settlers, since dog remains in Illinois are about ten thousand years old. Dogs hunted, guarded the camp, pulled sledges in the Arctic and kept their owners warm at night, and among the Coast Salish of the Pacific Northwest one breed was kept for its thick white wool. Its hair was spun and woven into blankets, but the breed died out after woven blankets from Europe became common.

The turkey was a native of North America, and it was domesticated in Mexico more than two thousand years ago, then kept by farmers in the Southwest as well. Cooks valued its meat and its eggs, while the people of the Pueblo cultures twisted turkey feathers around cords of yucca fibre to weave blankets that were light, soft and astonishingly warm. Such blankets were used by the living, and some of them have survived because they were laid in graves with their owners.

In the Andes, guinea pigs were not pets in the modern sense but a valuable source of meat that could be raised in the kitchen with almost no expense. These little animals, called cuy in Quechua, ate kitchen scraps and grass, and they were cooked for feasts and offered in religious ceremonies. Even today, roast cuy is a favourite dish for special occasions in Peru, Ecuador and Bolivia, where the animal is still raised in many homes.

Rivers and coasts were the highways of the Americas, and boat builders produced craft of every kind, including dugout canoes carved from single tree trunks, light birchbark canoes in the northern forests, and reed boats on Lake Titicaca. Mariners from Ecuador even sailed large balsa rafts with cotton sails along the Pacific coast, carrying cargoes of copper, shells and cloth. Such voyages tied together places that were hundreds of miles apart, and they helped ideas as well as goods to travel along the coast.

Long before Columbus, trade networks carried objects of beauty and value across thousands of miles of forest, desert and mountain. Turquoise from the Southwest reached the cities of Mexico, shells from the Gulf travelled far up the Mississippi, and obsidian from the Rocky Mountains has been found in Ohio more than a thousand miles from its source. The goods passed from hand to hand, so most traders knew only a short stretch of the road.

Caral lies in the Supe valley of Peru, in a dry landscape between the Pacific coast and the Andes, and it is about five thousand years old. It flourished at roughly the same time as the first cities of Mesopotamia and the pyramids of Egypt, though nobody in those places knew that it existed. Archaeologists have been studying it closely since the 1990s, and it is now recognised as one of the oldest cities in the Americas.

At the centre of Caral stand six huge platform mounds made of stone and earth, the largest of which is about eighteen metres high, together with a sunken circular plaza where crowds could gather. The people of the city used no pottery and left no writing that we can read, so everything we know comes from the buildings and the objects they left. Few signs of war have been found there, although the evidence is still being studied.

Caral was a city of farmers, and its fields along the river grew cotton, squash, beans and other crops with the help of irrigation canals. Fishers on the nearby coast caught enormous quantities of anchovies and sardines, and many scholars believe that the two groups traded with one another, since nets made of cotton were essential for fishing. The exchange may have helped to bind the whole region together, long before there were any kings, armies or written laws.

Among the most moving finds at Caral are thirty-two flutes made from the hollow wing bones of pelicans and other birds, some of them carved with tiny figures of animals. The musicians who played them performed at ceremonies on the great platforms, and the sound of the music must have carried across the valley on the evening air. Such instruments tell us that the city was a place of celebration as well as of work.

The temple of Chavin de Huantar, built in the high valleys of the Andes about three thousand years ago, drew pilgrims from across Peru, who came to honour its gods and to marvel at its carved stone heads. Inside the building, a maze of narrow stone passages leads to a tall carved stone called the Lanzon, which shows a figure with a human body and the fangs of a jaguar. Its style of art spread across the Andes and influenced many later peoples, who copied its fanged figures on their pottery and cloth.

On the arid south coast of Peru, the Paracas people buried their dead in bundles, wrapped in layer after layer of embroidered cloth that glows with red, yellow, blue and green. The desert is so dry that the fabrics survived for two thousand years, and their designs of birds, fish and spirit figures are among the finest textiles ever made. Weavers spent months and even years on a single cloth, and the work was treasured.

The Nazca people, who lived in the dry south of Peru from about two thousand years ago, made enormous drawings on the desert plain by clearing away the dark surface stones to reveal the pale earth beneath. Some of the figures, including a hummingbird and a monkey, are close to a hundred metres long, and they are seen best from the air or from nearby hills. Scholars still debate whether they were used for ritual, for walking in procession, or for water ceremonies.

Living in one of the driest places on Earth, the Nazca farmers found ways to tap the water that flowed beneath their valleys, and they dug channels called puquios to carry it to their fields. Each channel is marked at the surface by spiral openings that allowed people to reach in and clean it. Some of these ancient waterworks are still in use, so the engineering of the Nazca has outlasted their kingdom by many centuries.

On the north coast of Peru, the Moche built huge pyramids of sun-dried mud brick, such as the Huaca del Sol and the Huaca de la Luna, and watered their fields with long irrigation canals. Their potters made vessels in the shape of lifelike human faces, so we can see what some of the people of 1,500 years ago actually looked like. Their goldsmiths and weavers were equally gifted, and objects of gold and turquoise have been found in their tombs.

In 1987, the Peruvian archaeologist Walter Alva stopped looters from emptying a Moche tomb at Sipan, and then discovered that it held the burial of a powerful ruler, who had been laid to rest about 1,700 years ago. The lord was wearing gold ornaments, turquoise beads and a headdress, and he was surrounded by pottery, weapons and the bodies of the attendants who had been buried with him. The find showed how rich and highly organised Moche society had been, and it is now displayed in a museum built to hold its treasures.

Between about 3,200 and 2,400 years ago, the Olmec flourished on the hot and humid plains beside the Gulf of Mexico, where rivers flooded each year and left rich soil for farming. Their name is not what they called themselves but an Aztec word that means people of the rubber country. San Lorenzo was their first great centre, and La Venta, which stood further to the east, replaced it as the leading city about nine hundred years before the birth of Christ.

The most famous works of the Olmec are the seventeen colossal stone heads, each of which was carved from a single block of basalt and wears a close-fitting helmet. The tallest are more than three metres high and weigh many tonnes, and each face has its own particular features, as if the sculptor had known the person well. They stand today in museums and parks in the Mexican states of Veracruz and Tabasco.

The hard stone for the heads was quarried in the Tuxtla mountains, some fifty miles from the building sites, and it had to be moved without wheels, pack animals or metal tools. Archaeologists suspect that gangs of workers dragged the blocks on sledges and rolled them on logs, and that rafts carried them along the rivers. The effort must have involved hundreds of people, and it shows how much power the Olmec rulers commanded.

Because every head has its own face and its own style of helmet, most scholars believe that each one is a portrait of a particular ruler, perhaps carved after his death to keep his memory alive. A leader who could command the labour of so many people for such a task was clearly a person of enormous prestige. The heads were a message in stone about who ruled the land, and that message has lasted for more than two thousand years.

In the forests of southern Mexico, people collected the milky sap of the rubber tree and mixed it with the juice of a vine that grew nearby, which made the rubber stronger and more elastic. They used it to make balls, sandals, bands and waterproof coverings for their goods. Rubber balls about 3,600 years old have been found in a spring in Veracruz, long before Europeans had seen the substance.

One of the great pastimes of Mesoamerica was a ballgame played with a heavy rubber ball in a stone court shaped like the letter I. Players struck the ball with their hips and forearms, wore padded belts for protection, and tried to keep it moving without letting it touch the ground. Hundreds of ball courts have been found, and in some later cities the game was linked to religion and even to human sacrifice, although most matches were probably played for sport.

Besides their huge monuments, the Olmec produced exquisite small works in jade, the hard green stone that Mesoamericans valued above gold. Many figures have chubby, babyish faces and mouths that turn down like a snarling jaguar, and the same images appear in the art of later peoples, from the Maya to the Aztecs. The Olmec set patterns that would run through the arts of Mesoamerica for more than two thousand years.

Workers digging stone for a road in Veracruz in 1999 found a block of stone called the Cascajal Block, which is covered with sixty-two signs, some of them repeated, and which dates to about 900 years before the birth of Christ. Some scholars believe it is the earliest writing in the Americas, while others point out that a single object is not enough proof of a full writing system. For now, the meaning of the signs remains a mystery, and further discoveries will be needed before anyone can say for certain.

The Zapotec founded their capital of Monte Alban about 500 years before the birth of Christ, on the top of a mountain that overlooks the valleys of Oaxaca in southern Mexico. They levelled the summit to make room for plazas, temples, ball courts and tombs, and the city remained important for well over a thousand years. Carved stones there show some of the oldest writing and calendar signs in Mesoamerica.

Scholars use the name Mesoamerica for the region that stretches from central Mexico into Central America, where many peoples who spoke different languages shared a common set of customs. They farmed maize, played the ballgame, kept similar calendars, built stepped pyramids and traded cacao, jade and feathers along the same roads. They were never a single nation, but they were partners in a shared world that lasted for thousands of years.

The homeland of the Maya covered the hot lowlands of the Yucatan, the rainforests of Guatemala and Belize, and the cooler mountains to the south. They were never united in a single empire, but lived instead in dozens of independent city-states, each ruled by a king and each proud of its own gods and history. They shared a language family, a religion and a calendar, and they fought and traded with one another.

Long before the famous cities of the classic age, the Maya raised the great city of El Mirador in the northern jungle of Guatemala, where it flourished between about 300 years before Christ and the year 150. Its largest pyramid, La Danta, is one of the most massive buildings in the world, and wide stone causeways once connected it to nearby towns. Few visitors reach it today, because it can be approached only on foot or by helicopter.

Tikal, in the forests of Guatemala, was the most celebrated of the Maya cities, and at its height in the classic age it held tens of thousands of people. Its steep stone temples, painted red and crowned with carved roof combs, rose far above the trees, and the highest of them, Temple IV, still stands about seventy metres tall. The ruins are now a national park and one of the most visited places in Central America.

A Maya king was both a political leader and a sacred figure, who performed rituals, led armies and was believed to speak with the gods and ancestors on behalf of his people. The most powerful cities, Tikal and Calakmul, became long-standing rivals, and each gathered a circle of smaller allies around it. For hundreds of years their long struggle for power shaped the history of the whole Maya region, and the contest lasted until the classic age itself came to an end.

Pakal became king of Palenque as a boy of twelve in the year 615, and he ruled for sixty-eight years, building temples, palaces and a great reputation. In 1952, the Mexican archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier found a hidden stairway inside the Temple of the Inscriptions, and at the bottom of it lay Pakal's tomb, with a jade mask and a heavy carved stone lid. It remains one of the great discoveries of Maya archaeology, and the carved lid is still studied by scholars who disagree about its meaning.

Maya history is not only the story of kings, since several women held the power of rulers in their own right. Lady Yohl Iknal became the queen of Palenque in 583 and governed for twenty years, and Lady Six Sky arrived in the city of Naranjo in 682 and helped to rule it alongside her young son. Their names survive today only because Maya scribes carved them in stone and recorded the great events of their reigns for later readers.

The limestone lowlands of the Yucatan have almost no rivers or lakes, so the Maya had to find clever ways of surviving the long dry season. Engineers built stone-lined reservoirs and paved plazas that guided rainwater into storage, and communities also drew water from cenotes, the natural sinkholes that open in the limestone. Many cenotes were sacred, and people threw offerings of jade, pottery and gold into them.

Behind the splendour of the temples lived the great majority of Maya, who were farmers, potters, weavers and craftworkers living in houses of wooden poles and thatch built on low stone platforms. They planted maize, beans and squash in forest clearings, kept bees and orchards, and travelled into the city on market days to trade. Cacao beans were treasured as a kind of small change, as they were in the markets of central Mexico, and they could be used to buy food or cloth.

Maya artists painted with astonishing skill, and at Bonampak in the Mexican state of Chiapas the walls of three small rooms are covered in vivid scenes made about the year 790. They show noblemen in jaguar skins, musicians with rattles and drums, a fierce battle and the presentation of captives to a king. The blue paint of the murals has lasted for twelve centuries, and its colour is still stunning.

The finest Maya pottery was painted in rich reds, oranges and blacks with scenes of gods, kings, dancers and animals, and some vessels were made to hold the frothy chocolate that nobles drank. A number of painters were proud enough to sign their work, which shows that artists were respected members of society. Many of these vessels were buried in tombs, and they are now treasured in museums.

The Maya developed one of the most complete writing systems of the ancient Americas, with about eight hundred different signs arranged in neat square blocks. Some signs stood for whole words, while others represented syllables, so that a skilled scribe could spell out any word of the spoken language. They carved the signs in stone and wood, and they painted them on pottery, walls and books.

For centuries the Maya hieroglyphs were an unsolved puzzle, and many writers insisted that they could hold no history at all. In the 1950s the Russian scholar Yuri Knorozov showed that many signs stood for sounds, and in 1960 Tatiana Proskouriakoff proved that the inscriptions at one city told the births, marriages and victories of real kings. Today scholars can read most of the surviving texts, and every year new inscriptions are found that add something to the history.

Maya scribes also painted books on long strips of bark paper that were folded like a screen and covered with signs, tables and pictures. In 1562 the Spanish friar Diego de Landa ordered a great number of them burned in the town of Mani, because he thought that they were works of the devil. Only four of these books are known to survive today, and they are among the most valuable manuscripts in the world.

The city of Copan, in what is now Honduras, was famous for its Hieroglyphic Stairway, which climbs a temple on sixty-three steps carved with about 2,200 signs. This is the longest known inscription in the Maya world, and it tells the history of the city's dynasty from its beginning to the reign of the king who built it. In the nineteenth century, the stairs had fallen into a heap of stones, but archaeologists have since put them back.

Maya mathematicians wrote numbers with just three symbols, a dot for one, a bar for five and a shell for zero, and they counted in twenties instead of tens. The use of zero as a placeholder allowed them to write very large numbers with ease, and it appears in their inscriptions at least 1,700 years ago. Maya scholars invented it independently, with no help from India, where zero was developed in a different way.

Maya time was counted with two calendars at once, a sacred round of 260 days and a solar year of 365 days, which meshed together like cogwheels and returned to the same pairing only after fifty-two years. For longer spans, they used the Long Count, which numbered the days from a starting date set in the distant past, in the year 3114 before Christ. Every date in a Maya inscription could therefore be pinned down exactly, even if it recorded an event from many centuries before.

Without telescopes, Maya astronomers watched the sky for generations and discovered that the planet Venus returns to the same place every 584 days, which is very close to the true figure. They also compiled tables that helped them to predict eclipses of the sun and the moon, and the tables were copied into books such as the Dresden Codex. The movements of the heavens guided the timing of wars, planting and ceremonies, so that astronomy was part of daily life and of government.

In December 2012, many people feared that an ancient Maya prophecy was about to end the world, although no Maya text says anything of the kind. The Long Count had merely reached the end of one great cycle of about 5,125 years, a change that is much like an odometer turning over, and the Maya themselves wrote about dates far beyond that point. The day passed quietly, and life went on in the Maya towns and villages of Guatemala and Mexico exactly as it had before.

To be a scribe in a Maya city was to hold a position of honour, and many of the writers and painters came from noble families, including some of the king's own relatives. They learned to cut stone, paint with brushes made from animal hair, and prepare paper from the bark of fig trees. Their skills allowed the Maya to record events, count days and tell stories that would otherwise have been forgotten.

The Popol Vuh, a great book of the K'iche' Maya of Guatemala, was written in the Latin alphabet in the 1550s so that the old stories would not be lost. Its best-known tale follows the Hero Twins, who defeat the Lords of the Underworld in a ballgame and by their cleverness win their freedom and later rise into the sky. It also describes the creation of people from maize dough, a belief that is still remembered today.

About fifty kilometres from modern Mexico City, the people of Teotihuacan laid out their capital on a precise grid, with straight streets, great plazas and a vast central avenue. By the year 500 the city probably held more than a hundred thousand people, which made it one of the largest cities in the world at that time. Nobody knows what its builders called it, since the name we use was given by the Aztecs many centuries later.

At the heart of the city ran the Avenue of the Dead, a straight road that is more than two kilometres long, lined on both sides with temples, palaces and platforms. The Aztecs gave it that name because they believed the buildings beside it were tombs, but they were in fact places for ritual and government. To walk the avenue today is to feel the scale of the vanished city.

The Pyramid of the Sun, which was built about 1,800 years ago from earth, rubble and a skin of plaster, rises about sixty-five metres into the sky and is among the largest structures of the ancient Americas. At the northern end of the avenue stands the smaller Pyramid of the Moon, whose shape echoes the mountain behind it. Both were centres of ceremony, and thousands of people could gather in the plazas below.

The Temple of the Feathered Serpent is covered with carved snake heads that seem to burst from the stone, and in 2003 researchers discovered a tunnel that runs for about a hundred metres beneath it. Chambers at the end of the tunnel held thousands of offerings, among them jade figures, shells, pottery and balls of a yellow mineral. Scientists are still working out what these treasures can tell us about the beliefs of the city.

Archaeologists have found about two thousand walled apartment compounds in Teotihuacan, each one a cluster of rooms around courtyards, where extended families lived and worked together. The inner walls were covered with plaster and painted with murals of gods, animals, flowers and priests, some of which keep their colours after fifteen centuries. Many craftworkers lived in the compounds, and they made pottery, cloth and tools from black volcanic glass.

Texts carved at Tikal and other Maya cities tell us that a foreign lord called Siyaj Kak arrived in the year 378, and soon afterwards a new line of kings took the throne. Many scholars think that the newcomers were connected with Teotihuacan, because their monuments show warriors and symbols of that distant city. The event proves that the great city of the highlands could influence events nearly a thousand kilometres away.

Around the year 550, the central buildings of Teotihuacan were damaged by fire, and statues and carvings were smashed and burned along the great avenue. Some historians suspect an uprising against the rulers, others point to a long drought, and the truth may be a mixture of several causes. The city lost its power, although people continued to live among the ruins for many generations.

Between about the years 800 and 900, one Maya city after another stopped carving dates and raising new temples, and the great cities of the southern lowlands lost most of their people. Evidence from stalagmites in caves and from mud at the bottom of lakes shows that long and severe droughts struck the region, and these troubles came on top of war, crowded cities and exhausted soil. There was no single cause, and scholars still argue about how the different pressures combined.

While the southern cities faded, Chichen Itza in the northern Yucatan rose to wealth and power around the year 900, and its harbours on the coast carried goods as far as Central America. Its great pyramid, El Castillo, has 365 steps in all, and at the spring and autumn equinoxes the late sun throws a shadow on the stairs that looks like a snake wriggling down. The largest ball court in all of Mesoamerica lies beside the pyramid, and it measures about 168 metres from one end to the other.

It is a common mistake to speak of the Maya as a lost civilisation, because millions of Maya people live today in Mexico, Guatemala and Belize. Many of them speak one of about thirty Mayan languages at home, work as farmers and weavers, and keep customs that go back many centuries, including a calendar that is still used by some daily priests. The ruins are their ancestors' work, and they remain the guardians of that heritage.

Before the Inca ever came to power, the Andes had already seen the rise and fall of several great states, whose people lived in valleys so steep that a short walk could cross several climates. Tiwanaku, near Lake Titicaca, and Wari, in the highlands of Peru, were powerful between about the years 500 and 1000, and both built cities, terraces and roads. The Inca learned a great deal from the example of these earlier states, and they later copied many of their roads and farming methods.

The Chimu kingdom held the north coast of Peru from about the year 900, and its capital, Chan Chan, was the largest mud-brick city in the Americas, with walled palaces whose walls were carved with patterns of fish, birds and waves. Perhaps thirty thousand people lived there, among them goldsmiths and weavers of great skill. The Inca conquered the Chimu about 1470, and they took many of its craftworkers to Cusco.

Cusco lies in a green valley more than three thousand metres above the sea, and for a long time it was only one of several small kingdoms in the southern Andes. The Inca told stories about their beginnings in which the first ruler, Manco Capac, emerged from a cave or from the waters of Lake Titicaca, sent by the Sun to found a city. Historians treat such stories with care, but they show us how the Inca saw themselves.

Inca tradition says that around the year 1438 a powerful neighbour called the Chanka marched on Cusco, and that the city was saved by a prince named Pachacuti, who became ruler soon afterwards. His name means something like the one who turns the world over, and he began a series of conquests that changed the Andes. The details were recorded long after the events, so historians cannot be certain of every date.

Within about ninety years, Pachacuti, his son Topa Inca and his grandson Huayna Capac created the empire that its people called Tawantinsuyu, the four parts together, because it was divided into four quarters that met at Cusco. It stretched for about four thousand kilometres along the Andes, from what is now Ecuador and Colombia to Chile and Argentina. Perhaps ten million people lived within it, which made it the largest empire in the Americas.

The Inca expanded their empire by war but also by diplomacy, offering gifts and honours to local lords who accepted their rule, while crushing those who resisted. They also moved whole communities from one province to another, to settle new land and to keep watch over restless regions, and they made Quechua the common language of the empire. The sons of local leaders were taught in Cusco, so they grew up as loyal servants of the Inca state.

At the head of the empire stood the Sapa Inca, the only Inca, who wore a red fringe across his forehead and was believed to be a child of the Sun. When he died, his body was carefully mummified, and the mummy was kept in its own palace, served by attendants and carried out on feast days to take part in the ceremonies. Each dead ruler kept the estates that he had owned in life, and his family and attendants continued to manage them and to pay for the ceremonies.

The most honoured god of the Inca was Inti, the Sun, whose temple, the Coricancha, stood in the heart of Cusco, and whose rays were thought to give life to the whole empire. They also revered Viracocha, the creator of the world, and Pachamama, the Earth Mother, to whom farmers still make offerings in the Andes today. Spanish writers said that the walls of the Coricancha were covered with sheets of gold.

Each June, at the winter solstice in the southern hemisphere, the Inca held the festival of Inti Raymi to thank the Sun for the harvest and to ask it to return, with feasting, music, dancing and offerings. Spanish authorities forbade it after the conquest, but in the twentieth century the people of Cusco began to stage it again as a public festival. It is now one of the most popular celebrations in Peru, and visitors travel from all over the world to see the costumes and the processions.

The Inca valued cloth far more than gold, which they used for decoration rather than for money, because a fine garment represented months of skilled work. Expert weavers, many of them women, produced tunics in bright geometric patterns, and the state gave out such clothing to reward soldiers, win allies and honour the gods. A person's clothes showed at a glance where he or she came from and what rank he or she held.

The Inca road system, known as the Qhapaq Nan, ran for more than thirty thousand kilometres, linking the coast, the mountains and the edge of the jungle. Where the ground was steep the builders cut stairs into the rock, and on marshy ground they raised the road on a causeway with drains to carry off the rainwater. No wheeled cart ever travelled along them, since they were made for walkers and for llamas.

To cross the deep gorges of the Andes, Inca engineers twisted tough mountain grass into cables as thick as a man's body and hung them between stone towers, then laid a floor of sticks across the cables. The bridge at Q'eswachaka in Peru is still rebuilt each year by the local communities, using the same skills that their ancestors passed down. It is a living link with the Inca world, and each year the people of the nearby villages gather to weave the new cables by hand.

The Inca had no horses and no writing, yet news travelled with remarkable speed, carried by relay runners called chasqui who waited in small huts placed every few kilometres along the road. A runner would race to the next hut, give the message by voice or hand over a knotted cord, and rest while a fresh runner took it on. In this way, news could cross hundreds of kilometres in just a few days.

At intervals of roughly a day's walk, the road was punctuated by stations called tambos, which provided officials, messengers and soldiers with food, drink, firewood and a place to sleep. Their storerooms were filled by the surrounding villages as part of their duties to the state. Thanks to this system, an army could march for weeks through the mountains without carrying more than a small part of its own supplies.

Instead of writing, the Inca kept their accounts on quipus, bundles of dyed cords from which hung many smaller strings, tied with knots in different places. The position of each knot showed whether it counted ones, tens or hundreds, and the colour of the cord told what was being counted, such as people, llamas or sacks of maize. Some scholars think that quipus may also have recorded stories, but nobody has yet shown how to read that kind of message.

In an empire without money or markets, taxes were paid in labour, and under the system called the mita each household owed the state a share of its time. People built roads, worked the state's fields, served in the army or wove cloth, and in return the state fed them and held great feasts with maize beer. The arrangement rested on the idea of fair exchange between the people and the ruler.

On the hillsides above Inca towns stood long rows of stone storehouses, built where the cold, dry wind would help to preserve the food inside. They were packed with maize, freeze-dried potatoes, cloth, weapons and tools, and the stores were opened to feed armies, workers and villages in times of famine. A government that could store and share food in this way was a powerful government indeed, and its subjects had good reason to support it.

Wherever the land was too steep to farm, the Inca built terraces, stone-walled steps that held the soil and carried irrigation water carefully from one level to the next. At Moray, near Cusco, huge circular terraces sink into the ground like a bowl, and the temperature differences between the levels may have allowed farmers to test crops in different climates. The terraces are still farmed today, and some have been in use for five hundred years.

Inca builders shaped enormous stones, some weighing more than a hundred tonnes, and set them together so precisely that a knife blade cannot be slipped between them, without any mortar to bind them. They also made doorways and windows slightly narrower at the top, and walls that lean a little inward, which helped their buildings to survive earthquakes. Some Inca walls in Cusco still stand firm, while later Spanish buildings have repeatedly been damaged.

Machu Picchu was built in the middle of the fifteenth century on a high ridge above the Urubamba River, most likely as a royal estate for Pachacuti and his family. A few hundred people lived there, tending terraces and serving the court, and it was left empty not long after the arrival of the Spanish. Local farmers had always known about the place, but the American explorer Hiram Bingham made it famous to the world in 1911.

Around the thirteenth century, a people who called themselves the Mexica arrived in the Valley of Mexico, where older cities had already taken the best land around the lakes. Their own histories say that they had travelled from a legendary homeland called Aztlan, which is where the later name Aztec comes from. They spoke Nahuatl, and for many years they were poor strangers who sold their services as fighters to stronger neighbours.

The Mexica told how their war god Huitzilopochtli had promised them a home in a place where they saw an eagle perched upon a prickly pear cactus, and they found the sign on a muddy island in Lake Texcoco.  There they founded their city of Tenochtitlan around the year 1325, in a spot that nobody else wanted because it was swampy and surrounded by water. The eagle on the cactus appears today on the flag of Mexico, so that the old story of the founding is seen every day by millions of people.

Over the following century, the Mexica turned their island into a capital by building three great causeways across the lake, with gaps that could be crossed on wooden bridges, and by digging canals through the city for canoes. A long dike protected the freshwater parts of the lake from the salty waters, and an aqueduct from the hill of Chapultepec brought clean drinking water to the people. All of this was done without iron tools, without wheeled carts and without any draft animals, by the strength and skill of the workers alone.

When Spanish soldiers first saw Tenochtitlan in 1519, it held perhaps two hundred thousand people, more than almost any city in Europe at the time, with white temples, towers and houses rising from the middle of a lake. One of them, Bernal Diaz del Castillo, later wrote that some of the men wondered whether it was a dream, since nothing in their experience had prepared them for such a sight. Most of them had come across the ocean expecting to find only villages, and instead they found a city of a size that they could hardly describe.

To feed so many people, the farmers of the lakes built chinampas, narrow rectangular plots made from layers of mud and water plants and held in place by willow trees planted around the edge. The soil stayed moist from the water on every side, and the farmers fertilised it with mud from the canals, so they could grow maize, beans, squash, chilli and flowers three or even four times a year. Some chinampas near Mexico City, in the district of Xochimilco, are still farmed today, and the canals are a popular place for visitors to ride in boats.

The great market of Tlatelolco, in the twin city beside Tenochtitlan, sold nearly everything that could be grown, made or hunted, including maize, feathers, pottery, cloth, obsidian blades, herbs and gold. The Spanish leader Hernan Cortes reported that sixty thousand people visited it each day, and although this may be an exaggeration, it was clearly enormous. Officials walked through the stalls to settle quarrels and to check that the weights and measures were fair.

In 1428 the Mexica made an alliance with two other cities, Texcoco and Tlacopan, and together they defeated a powerful rival and began to conquer neighbouring peoples. They did not govern those peoples directly, but demanded tribute in the form of cloth, food, cacao, feathers and soldiers, and a painted book called the Codex Mendoza lists these payments in detail. The system made the capital rich and powerful, although it also made many enemies among the peoples who were forced to pay.

Education was taken seriously in the Aztec world, and many boys went to school in their teens. Boys from ordinary families learned the arts of war and public work in a school called the telpochcalli, while the sons of nobles studied history, religion and the reading of painted books in the calmecac. Girls were mostly taught at home by their mothers, though some also served in the temples as helpers and learned the songs of the gods.

The Stone of the Sun is carved from a single block of volcanic rock about three and a half metres wide. At its centre is a face that most scholars identify as the sun, surrounded by signs for the days and ages of the world. It was carved in the early 1500s and was found buried beneath the main square of Mexico City in 1790, and today it is one of the most famous objects in the National Museum of Anthropology.

At the centre of Tenochtitlan stood the Templo Mayor, a double pyramid for the war god Huitzilopochtli and the rain god Tlaloc, where priests held the most solemn ceremonies of the empire. The Aztecs practised human sacrifice because they believed that the gods needed it to keep the world going, and excavations have confirmed that it happened, though Spanish writers probably exaggerated the numbers. Modern historians try to describe the practice honestly and with care, without any shock for effect and without making any excuses for it.

At Watson Brake, beside a river in Louisiana, the people of the Archaic age raised a ring of eleven earth mounds linked by low ridges, about five thousand years ago. They lived by hunting, fishing and gathering, and they had no crops or cities, yet they were willing to carry thousands of baskets of soil to make a place of meeting. It is one of the oldest mound sites known in North America, and it shows that complex building did not need farming or cities.

Poverty Point, which dates from about 3,400 years ago, is a giant set of six curved earth ridges, one inside the other, around a central plaza, with mounds standing beyond. It was built by hunting and fishing communities that traded stone and minerals from hundreds of miles away, and archaeologists estimate that the workers moved millions of baskets of soil. The site was named a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 2014, and visitors can now walk along the ridges.

Between about 100 years before Christ and the year 500, the peoples whom archaeologists call the Hopewell built dozens of enormous earthworks in the valleys of Ohio, including perfect circles, squares and octagons that sometimes joined together. Some of these shapes were nearly a kilometre across, and they were made with simple tools such as digging sticks and baskets. The name Hopewell comes from the farmer on whose land the first mounds were studied, not from the people themselves.

At Newark in Ohio, the builders arranged an octagon of earth so that its openings line up with the points where the moon rises and sets over a cycle that lasts a little more than eighteen years. It shows that the Hopewell had watched the sky patiently for generations and that they planned their buildings with an astronomer's care. In 2023, UNESCO listed the Hopewell earthworks as a World Heritage Site, so that they will be protected for the future.

The Hopewell world was linked by exchange across a huge area, and the objects buried in its mounds came from distant lands. Copper was brought from the shores of Lake Superior, shells from the Gulf of Mexico, shining sheets of mica from the Appalachian hills and obsidian from the Rocky Mountains, and craftsmen turned them into ornaments, tools and ritual pipes. These treasures were laid in the graves of respected people, and they show how far the Hopewell world reached.

Beside the Mississippi, across the river from the modern city of St Louis, the city of Cahokia expanded rapidly after about the year 1050, and within a generation or two it had become the greatest city north of Mexico. Its population around 1100 was probably between ten thousand and twenty thousand, with many more living in the nearby villages. Even then it remained a place of mystery, since its people had no writing.

At the centre of Cahokia stands Monks Mound, which rises about thirty metres in several terraces and covers more area at its base than the Great Pyramid of Egypt. It was made over many years by workers who carried baskets of soil on their backs, and a large building, perhaps a temple or a ruler's house, once stood on its summit. Its name comes from French monks who lived and farmed nearby in the early 1800s, long after the city itself had been abandoned.

Close to the great mound, the builders of Cahokia set up circles of tall wooden posts, which modern scholars have named Woodhenge, and on days such as the equinoxes the sun rises exactly in line with certain posts. The city also had a large open plaza, where crowds watched chunkey, a game in which players threw spears at a rolling stone disk. Both the sky and the game seem to have mattered a great deal to the people of Cahokia.

In the 1960s, archaeologists digging in a low mound at Cahokia discovered the grave of a man who had been laid on a cape of about twenty thousand shell beads arranged in the outline of a bird. Around him were the remains of many other people, some of whom may have been sacrificed for the occasion, along with copper, mica and arrowheads from far away. It shows that Cahokia had powerful leaders and rituals that we can only partly understand.

By about the year 1350, the people of Cahokia had left their great city, and the grass was growing over its plazas about a century before Columbus was born. Scholars suspect a mixture of causes, including floods, drought, conflict and the cutting of too many trees, though no single explanation has won agreement. Native nations of the region today consider the builders of Cahokia to be their ancestors.

The Southwest is a land of red cliffs, flat-topped mesas and deep canyons, where rain is scarce and unreliable, yet the ancestors of today's Pueblo peoples built a thriving society there. They grew corn, beans and squash, raised turkeys, and guided the water of sudden storms into their fields with small dams and ditches. Their skill at saving water was the foundation of everything else that they achieved, from their villages to their festivals and their art.

Between about the years 850 and 1150, the builders of Chaco Canyon in New Mexico raised a series of great stone houses. The largest of them, Pueblo Bonito, grew in stages until it had hundreds of rooms and stood up to four storeys high, and for centuries it was the biggest building in North America. Its walls were made of thin sandstone blocks set in clay, laid with great skill and precision.

Many buildings at Chaco Canyon seem to have been laid out in relation to the sun and the moon. On the high rock of Fajada Butte, slivers of sunlight once fell across spirals carved in the stone at the solstices, an effect known as the Sun Dagger that erosion has now disturbed. Scholars still debate how much of it was intended by the people who made the carvings.

From Chaco Canyon, a network of roads ran out across the desert and the mesas, often in straight lines for many miles, and they were cut into the rock or built up with stone where the ground was uneven. They were about nine metres wide, which is far wider than people on foot would require, so their purpose may have been ceremonial. None of them was ever used by a wheeled cart, because the people of the Southwest had neither the wheel nor the animals to pull it.

Although Chaco lay in a desert, its great houses were full of things from far away, including the feathers and skeletons of scarlet macaws from Mexico, turquoise ornaments and pottery jars that held traces of chocolate. The builders also hauled tens of thousands of pine and fir timbers for their roofs from mountains at least fifty miles away, using nothing but human muscle. A place that needed so many resources must have been a centre of great importance to the whole region.

In the middle of the twelfth century, tree rings tell us that a long and severe drought hit the Southwest, and the great houses of Chaco Canyon lost their authority and their people. Families moved north and south, carrying their traditions with them and founding new communities. Chaco was never forgotten, and it has remained a sacred place for the Pueblo peoples and the Navajo Nation to the present day.

At Mesa Verde in Colorado, the Ancestral Pueblo people built stone villages into the sheltered hollows of the canyon cliffs, and most of them were constructed between about the years 1190 and 1260. The largest of these, Cliff Palace, held about a hundred and fifty rooms and twenty-three kivas, which were round underground rooms used for ceremonies and meetings. Reaching them required climbing up and down the rock using handholds and ladders, and children grew up learning to do so with ease.

Between about the years 1276 and 1299, a severe drought dried up the springs and crops of Mesa Verde, and the families who had lived in the cliff villages for generations began to leave. They moved south, towards the Rio Grande and the mesas of Arizona and New Mexico, where water was easier to find. Their descendants today live in the Pueblo communities, who say clearly that their ancestors never vanished.
