In the Sonoran Desert of southern Arizona, the Hohokam people dug hundreds of miles of irrigation canals, with no tools except digging sticks and stone hoes, to bring water from the Salt River to their fields. These canals made it possible to grow crops in one of the hottest places in North America, and they supported large villages for more than a thousand years. Some of the routes were reused by the modern city of Phoenix, which was built on the same plain and still follows some of the old routes.

The Pueblo peoples did not vanish, and several of their villages are still lived in after many centuries, among them Acoma, the Hopi villages and Taos Pueblo in New Mexico. Taos has been home to families for about a thousand years, and its multi-storey houses of earth are replastered by the people each year as they always have been. The community was listed as a World Heritage Site in 1992, and its residents continue to welcome visitors while keeping many of their ceremonies private.

The forests of eastern North America, stretching from the Great Lakes to the Atlantic coast and south toward the Gulf of Mexico, were home to many nations who spoke languages of several different families. Peoples such as the Haudenosaunee, the Cherokee, the Wampanoag and the Muscogee lived in villages and towns, farmed maize, beans and squash, and hunted and fished the rich waters. Each nation had its own government and its own traditions, and each also had a strong sense of belonging to the land that it had always known.

The Haudenosaunee, whose name means the people of the longhouse, built long, narrow houses on frames of bent poles, covered with sheets of elm bark. Some were more than thirty metres long and sheltered many related families, each with its own hearth along the central corridor. The five nations lived in what is now New York State, and they were the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca.

Among the Haudenosaunee, a child belonged to the clan of its mother, and the longhouse was the property of the women who lived there. Women directed the farming, owned the harvest and shared the food, and the senior women of each clan, known as clan mothers, chose the men who served as chiefs and could remove them if they failed in their duties. This gave women a political voice that was unusual in the world of 1491, when most of the societies of Europe gave them very little say in public affairs.

The Haudenosaunee tell that their five nations were once locked in cycles of revenge and war, until a visionary known as the Peacemaker arrived with his spokesman, Hiawatha, and persuaded the nations to stop fighting. Estimates of the date range from about the year 1100 to as late as the 1500s, and scholars have not agreed on the answer. The story is still told with great care and respect by the Haudenosaunee, who regard it as the foundation of their nation.

The Great Law of Peace, which the Peacemaker taught, set up a grand council of fifty chiefs drawn from the five nations, and it laid down rules for how they should meet and decide. Its best-known symbol is the Tree of Peace, a great white pine beneath whose roots the nations buried their weapons of war. Some historians believe that the Great Law was one of the inspirations of later democratic ideas, though this remains debated.

Wampum was made from small beads of white and purple shell, which were threaded onto strings and woven into belts in careful patterns that carried meaning. They recorded treaties, laws and important events, and a trained speaker would hold a belt and recite the words that it called to mind. A wampum belt could not be forged easily, and so it served as a reliable witness to a promise.

A meeting of the Haudenosaunee began with a Thanksgiving Address, a long speech in which the speaker thanks the people, the earth, the waters, the plants, the animals, the winds, the sun and the moon in turn. The leaders then debated an issue for as long as necessary, aiming to reach an agreement that everyone could accept instead of simply voting. The Thanksgiving Address is still spoken in Haudenosaunee communities today, at the start of meetings and school days.

Across eastern North America, many peoples set low, controlled fires in the woods to clear the undergrowth, which produced open, park-like forests where deer, wild turkeys, berries and nut trees thrived. Early European visitors often remarked that they could ride a horse between the trees, without realising that people had made the landscape that way. What they took for untouched nature was in fact a carefully managed landscape, shaped by many generations of people with fire.

In the lakes of the north, the Ojibwe and their neighbours harvested wild rice by gliding in canoes through the water plants and knocking the ripe grains into the boat, leaving enough seed in the water for the next year. On the prairies to the west, communities burned the grass to encourage fresh green growth that would draw the bison. Both practices show how carefully peoples managed the plants and animals they depended on.

Between 1539 and 1543, the Spanish explorer Hernando de Soto led an army through the southeastern part of what is now the United States, and his men described large towns, well-tended fields and chiefs who were carried in litters. When French explorers travelled the same region more than a century later, they found far fewer people, and some of the towns had vanished altogether. Historians think that disease, war and disruption were the main reasons, though the full story of what happened is still being pieced together.

On the rainy Pacific coast between Alaska and Oregon, enormous runs of salmon returned to the rivers each year. The peoples there, among them the Haida, the Tlingit and the Coast Salish, caught, smoked and stored the fish in vast quantities, and their abundance supported large villages, skilled artists and complex societies. It is a striking example of a rich civilisation that was built without any farming at all.

The cedar tree was the cornerstone of life on the Northwest Coast, supplying planks for houses, logs for canoes that could carry dozens of people, and soft inner bark that was pounded and woven into clothes, hats and baskets. Often the planks were split from living trees, which survived the cutting and kept growing. The art of the carpenter and the carver was held in great respect, and master craftsmen were sometimes paid with valuable gifts.

In front of the great plank houses stood tall cedar poles carved with animals and other beings, such as ravens, eagles, bears and killer whales, which served as the crests of a family or clan. Each pole told the history of a family, recorded a marriage or an event, or honoured a person who had died, and the images were read much as a book is read. They were works of art as well as records, and a great pole could take a skilled carver and his helpers many months to complete.

At a potlatch, a family invited neighbouring communities to a great feast with music, dancing and speeches, and it gave away gifts of blankets, copper shields, carved boxes and food. The guests became witnesses to the family's claims, such as a new name, a marriage or the right to use a crest, and generous giving earned a family great respect. In the late nineteenth century governments tried to ban the potlatch, but the tradition survived.

The ancestors of the Inuit, sometimes called the Thule people, began to move east from Alaska about a thousand years ago, following whales and seals along the northern shore of the continent. Within a few centuries they had spread across the Arctic coast of Canada as far as Greenland, adapting their way of life to every kind of ice and sea. They built houses of stone, turf and whalebone and, in some places, of snow.

The kayak was one of the most ingenious inventions of the Arctic, a narrow boat with a frame of driftwood or whalebone covered with carefully sewn sealskin, and an opening in the middle for the hunter. It was almost silent and very fast, and it allowed a skilled paddler to creep up on seals, while larger open boats called umiaks carried whole families. Warm parkas of caribou fur and sealskin, sewn with tiny stitches by the women of the family, protected people from the harshest winds.

To survive in the Arctic, the Inuit developed a detailed knowledge of the ice, the weather and the animals, and a hunter might spend hours beside a hole in the sea ice, waiting for a seal to surface and breathe. Travellers found their way across the featureless snow by reading the direction of the wind, the pattern of the snowdrifts and the position of the stars. Such knowledge was handed down from parents to children through stories and long practice.

The Amazon rainforest was far from empty before the arrival of the Europeans, for large communities lived on the bluffs beside the rivers, growing cassava, peanuts and fruit trees and catching fish and turtles. In the Upper Xingu region of Brazil, archaeologists have found clusters of villages arranged around circular plazas and joined to one another by wide, straight roads and ditches. These places were home to thousands of people, and archaeologists have traced the lines of the old roads and ditches through the forest.

The soils of the Amazon are mostly thin and poor, yet in many places there are patches of terra preta, a dark and fertile earth created over generations by the people who lived there. They mixed charcoal, broken pottery, fish bones and plant waste into the ground, and the result stays rich for hundreds of years. Modern scientists study terra preta closely, hoping to learn how to improve farmland and trap carbon in the soil.

When part of the western Amazon was cleared of trees in recent decades, researchers saw hundreds of huge squares, circles and ditches in the ground, which local people dug mostly between about two thousand and eight hundred years ago. Studies also show that useful trees, such as the Brazil nut and the cacao tree, are more common near ancient settlements, as if they had been planted deliberately. The rainforest is not a pure wilderness but a landscape shaped partly by human care.

Around the year 1000, Viking sailors from Greenland crossed the cold sea to Newfoundland, nearly five hundred years before Columbus, and built a small camp of turf-walled houses at L'Anse aux Meadows. The site was found by Norwegian explorers in 1960, and a study of tree rings in 2021 showed that the Norse were cutting wood there in the year 1021. It is the earliest known European presence in the Americas, and it is now protected as a World Heritage Site that visitors can walk around.

The Norse stories, known as sagas, describe a brief and difficult meeting with the local people, whom the newcomers called Skraelings, and they say that quarrels broke out and some people were killed. The visitors were few and far from home, and they stayed for only a few years before they sailed away. As a result, the people of the Americas and the people of Europe remained unknown to one another until the voyage of Columbus.

Christopher Columbus, a sailor from Genoa in Italy, spent years trying to convince the rulers of Europe that Asia could be reached by sailing west across the Atlantic. His calculations were wrong, since he believed that the earth was far smaller than it really is, and he had no idea that two continents stood in the way. In 1492 the king and queen of Spain finally agreed to pay for the voyage.

Columbus left the Spanish port of Palos in August 1492 with three small ships called the Nina, the Pinta and the Santa Maria, and about ninety men. After a stop in the Canary Islands to repair a rudder, they sailed west across open ocean for more than a month, while the sailors grew increasingly worried that they would never see land again. At last, in the early morning of the twelfth of October, a lookout cried that he could see the shore.

Columbus waded ashore on the twelfth of October 1492 on a small island in the Bahamas, and he claimed it for Spain without asking the people who had lived there for centuries. The islanders, who were called the Taino, knew the island as Guanahani, and the Spanish newcomers renamed it San Salvador. Scholars still disagree about exactly which of the many islands of the Bahamas it was, and several of them have been proposed over the years.

The Taino lived in villages of round wooden houses, each led by a chief known as a cacique, and they grew cassava, maize, sweet potatoes and cotton in mounded gardens and caught fish from the sea. English has borrowed several words from their language, including canoe, hammock, hurricane and barbecue. Their sailing canoes could carry dozens of people between the islands of the Caribbean.

In his own journal, Columbus wrote that the islanders were friendly and generous, and that they traded cotton thread and parrots for little glass beads and bells. At the same time he noted that they would make good servants, he searched anxiously for signs of gold, and he took some of the people on board his ships against their will. These private notes give an early hint of the harshness that was to follow, and they show what he really thought of the people he met.

When Columbus returned to Spain with news of the lands he had found, the court at once organised a larger voyage, and in 1493 he sailed again with seventeen ships and more than a thousand men. Besides soldiers, priests and farmers, the fleet carried horses, cattle, pigs and sugar cane, none of which had ever been seen in the Americas. Nothing in the two continents would ever be the same again, because every one of those animals and plants would change the land.

The ships brought a hidden danger, for the Europeans carried smallpox, measles, influenza and other infections that had never before reached the Americas. Because nobody there had ever been exposed to them, nobody had any immunity, and the diseases swept through villages and towns with terrible force. The epidemics often moved faster than the Europeans themselves, travelling along trade routes into lands where no foreigner had yet been seen.

On the island of Hispaniola, where the Spanish first settled, the Taino population declined sharply within a few decades, as smallpox arrived about 1518 and the colonists forced people to work in mines and fields. Historians cannot agree how many people lived there at the start, since estimates run from tens of thousands to over a million, but all agree that the losses were enormous. By the middle of the century, only small groups remained on the island, and their descendants and their words survive in the Caribbean today.

In 1519, the Spanish captain Hernan Cortes landed on the coast of Mexico with about five hundred soldiers, some horses and a few cannons. A woman called Malinche served as his translator, and he soon discovered that many peoples, above all the people of Tlaxcala, were bitter enemies of the Mexica and willing to fight beside him. Without these allies, he could not possibly have succeeded, and most historians agree that they were the main part of his army.

On the eighth of November 1519, the Mexica ruler Moctezuma came out along the great causeway to meet Cortes, and he welcomed the Spanish into Tenochtitlan with courtesy and with gifts. Within a few days, however, Cortes had taken him prisoner in his own palace, and the situation grew steadily more dangerous for everybody in the city. Both sides were afraid, and neither side fully understood the other, so a peaceful meeting soon turned into a bitter and violent struggle.

In the spring of 1520, after a Spanish attack on a festival, the people of Tenochtitlan rose against the strangers, and Moctezuma died during the fighting, although accounts differ about who was responsible. The Spanish fled along the causeways on the night of June 30, in an escape that they called the Night of Sorrows, and they lost hundreds of men. Within months a smallpox epidemic swept through the city and killed many thousands of its people.

In 1521, Cortes returned with tens of thousands of Indigenous warriors from Tlaxcala and other cities, together with a fleet of small ships built to carry soldiers onto the lake. The siege of Tenochtitlan lasted about seventy-five days, and hunger, disease and fighting brought the city down in August, when its last ruler, Cuauhtemoc, was captured. The Spanish then built a new capital, Mexico City, on the ruins of the old one, and the modern city still stands on the same site today.

In 1532, Francisco Pizarro arrived in Peru with fewer than two hundred men, at a moment when the Inca empire was exhausted by a civil war between two sons of Huayna Capac, Atahualpa and Huascar. At Cajamarca, the Spanish ambushed the victorious Atahualpa and took him prisoner, and in return for his freedom he promised them a room full of gold and silver. Epidemics had already weakened the empire, but the Spanish killed him in 1533 all the same, and the empire soon fell into their hands.

When Cusco fell to the Spanish, a group of Inca nobles retreated to the mountain stronghold of Vilcabamba, where they kept the old ways and resisted the invaders for nearly forty years. The last of their rulers, Tupac Amaru, was captured and executed in 1572, and the Spanish colony then took firm control of the Andes. Even so, the Quechua language and many Inca customs survived among the people of the mountains.

In the regions that suffered most, the number of people fell by half or more within a century, although the true figures are unknown and some scholars believe the losses were greater still. Some scientists have suggested that forests growing back across abandoned farmland pulled so much carbon from the air that the climate cooled slightly, but this idea is still debated. Whatever the truth, it is a reminder that a human catastrophe can leave its mark on the planet.

Modern science has given us new ways to see the past, and one of the most powerful is lidar, a laser survey from aircraft that can map the ground beneath a thick forest. A survey in Guatemala in 2018 revealed more than sixty thousand Maya buildings, roads and fields that nobody had noticed, and DNA studies and tree rings are adding evidence of their own. The best researchers now work with Indigenous communities, whose oral histories offer clues that no instrument can find.

The first peoples of the Americas did not vanish, and their descendants, numbering tens of millions, live today in every country of both continents. Millions of them speak languages such as Quechua, Nahuatl, Guarani and the many Mayan tongues, and they keep alive farming methods, festivals, crafts and stories that stretch back thousands of years. They have also created modern cities, universities and governments, and many are working to protect their languages and their land.

The history of the Americas did not begin with Columbus, for these were lands of cities, farms, observatories and nations long before 1492. Their gifts to the world, including maize, potatoes, tomatoes, chocolate and rubber, are with us every day, and their descendants remain among us. To know that older story is to see the whole world, and the people who live in it, a little more fairly.
